speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is certainly a great pleasure and an honour to be speaking in the House of Commons for the first time, and I take this opportunity to convey the respectful sentiments of my constituents in Nunatsiaq. I congratulate the respective members of the House on their election and you, Mr. Speaker, on your re-election to the chair.
1 also congratulate the New Democratic Party on being receptive to having a member from the eastern Arctic among their number. When my riding is included the NDP represents a good one third of the geographic extent of Canada.
1 would also like to commend my predecessor, Mr. Walley Firth, for his hard work and dedicated service as member for the Northwest Territories, including the western Arctic, during the six years preceding the Thirty-first Parliament.
Mr. Speaker, the Northwest Territories, and especially my riding of Nunatsiaq, traditionally and historically occupied by lnuit, has been terra incognita to the rest of the world. Unknown, menacing and certainly too cold for civilized habitation, it is only recently, in the last few decades, that something of national interest in the north has taken place. This is not because of the people who live there but because the possibilities of economic development in the extractive industries promise to be profitable.
In this light, it was only in 1960 that the lnuit were given the right to vote in Canada and we have that great gentleman and parliamentarian, the late Right Hon. John G. Diefen-baker, to thank for that inestimable right. Perhaps I might put this attitude toward relations between my people and the Government of Canada in its true perspective by quoting two people. The first is the former commissioner of the Northwest Territories, Stuart M. Hodgson, who said:
The emergence of the Northwest Territories as a political and economic force promises to be the twentieth century's greatest saga. It will include industrial development on a scale suited to the size of the land, giving employment to thousands of modern pioneers. It will be a modern re-enactment of old frontier days-accelerated and magnified by world pressures of population, increased commercial demands and heightened by competition for mineral resources. It will be rocketed ahead by computer-oriented technology.
These immortal words were uttered in an atmosphere of prophetic elation in 1970. I would like now to quote one of my own people on the same subject and please understand, Mr. Speaker, that the use of the word "white" is not meant in a derogatory sense. Please do not feel slighted.
We very much dislike white people taking our land for granted. It seems they feel they can destroy our land any time they feel like it without even asking for permission. We want to have freedom of conservation with the animals. They steal the raw materials without even consulting us or giving the lnuit a percentage of what they are taking. We need to get power to control the land.
These were the words of Elijah Takkiapik spoken in 1974. The desire for control is very real today among the lnuit of Canada.
My riding of Nunatsiaq is the largest in Canada and also one of the most distinctive. It is one of only three ridings-
[Mr. Deniger.J
perhaps soon there will only be two-in which the people who were born there, and who make it their home, have virtually no democratic voice in the management of their affairs.
While it is true that we have a territorial council situated in the western Arctic in Yellowknife, this council is subject to the authority of the territorial commissioner who is not elected and is himself under the authority of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Epp), and I see him across the way. How do you do?
I wish to spend the next few minutes outlining some of the specific regional problems faced by the people in my constituency. At a time when one can fly to Paris, France in less than ten hours, it often takes two days to travel from Ottawa to my home in Rankin Inlet. This increases the feeling that northern people have of being isolated from the rest of their country, but it also has serious economic consequences. The unusually high cost of living is due to increasingly high transportation costs and inadequate transportation services. A review of northern transportation is greatly needed. I am sure a review would lead to the implementation of a northern transportation subsidy or alternate means of alleviating the burden of these high costs.
To give some idea of the costs in the north, I am going to quote a couple of prices given to me yesterday from Frobisher Bay. Frobisher Bay, by the way, is the first port of call for air and sea transport in the Northwest Territories, so these would be the least costly consumer items in all Northwest Territories communities, aside from the western Arctic. Bread costs up to $2 a loaf. Reconstituted milk in Frobisher Bay costs $3.40 for two quarts and the bargain price of $6.98 for four litres. I dare not mention the price of home heating oil or gasoline because that is a joke.
Concurrent with the high cost of living is the fact that native employment is disproportionately low. The administration, which attracts many outsiders to high-paying bureaucratic jobs, has been inadequate in the area of job-training programs for local residents. Poor education and lack of adequate jobtraining leads naturally to low employment rates. At the same time our traditional livelihood-hunting, fishing and trapping-has been jeopardized by haphazard development and such regulatory controls as the Migratory Birds Convention Act, the northwest territorial government game ordinance, and so forth.
One point I would like to emphasize is that the lnuit are not generally opposed to development per se. What we are opposed to is the rapid, untimely development which has been externally imposed on us; development which endangers our land, our people, our way of life; development which benefits the residents of southern Canada and which benefits even the country of West Germany in the case of uranium mining-or at least they propose such development with the help of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development-and finally, development which leaves the residents of the Arctic to deal with the social and environmental consequences on their own.

October 16, 1979
I would like now to quote a former prime minister of Canada, Mr. Louis St. Laurent, who stated:
It has been said that Great Britain acquired her empire in a state of absence of mind. Apparently, we have administered these vast territories of the north in an almost continuing absence of mind.
This absence of mind has been demonstrated in the past by an attitude which sees the north as a boundless storehouse of resources juSt waiting to be exploited. This attitude has resulted in political and economic development which has ignored the cultural, social and political rights of native people and has denied them the opportunity to participate fully in the processes which are shaping their future.
The creation of the department of northern affairs and national resources in 1953 officially placed control of the north in the hands of bureaucrats, and this trend has continued through the devolution of the present Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. The creation of the territorial council has done little to change this, as most major decisions are still made in Ottawa. Current government policy regarding the north seems vague and full of contradictions. At least, this is my interpretation after listening to the Speech from the Throne and a number of comments made by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
1 would like for a few minutes to comment on the push for mining development as mentioned in the throne speech. In fact, that was all that was mentioned in the speech about the far north. Let me retrace our steps for a moment. The northern mineral advisory committee was formed under the auspices of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development of the old Liberal government. It consists of 15 members chosen exclusively from government and the mining industry.
Its mandate was to advise the minister in formulating policies and strategies for the development of the mining industry in the Yukon and Northwest Territories. It is, therefore, an instrument of the previous government and was to be used in the formation of Liberal policies. The present government has promised early action on the recommendations made by this committee in its recently released report. The Conservative government has therefore presumably adopted what would otherwise have been Liberal policy and has done so despite many inadequacies in the committee's recommendations, some of which I would like to point out.
This report ignores the broad implications of its mandate in favour of the narrow, vested interests of the mining industry. No discussions were held with members of any of the native organizations or any other special interest groups in the territories-and there are quite a few-and although participation of northern residents is given token consideration, the report states that, and 1 quote:
-its achievement must be coupled by an equally strong effort by industry to adapt the particular characteristics and strengths of northern people to the needs of industry.
I hesitate to say what the people up north would call that.
Furthermore, the report ignores the fact that a dispute over uranium mining in the Baker Lake area is now before the
The Address-Mr. Ittinuar
courts and that little information is available about the nature of industry-government negotiations concerning Cominco's proposed Arvik mine on Little Cornwallis Island. The uneasy conclusion is that policy is being formed by industry and government behind closed doors. Such approaches to development decision-making can only heighten suspicion and mistrust, and that is the process going on now.
I would like to draw the attention of the House to certain inconsistencies and inaccuracies which cast further doubt on the validity of this report as a basis for government policy. The report states, and I quote:
Mining can be a most effective vehicle for increased economic activity and opportunity for employment and training for all people now living in the north or wishing some day to settle there.
Unfortunately, the record of native employment at such mines as Pine Point, Cyprus Anvil and Nanisivik has been dismal. Also, mining in the territories has to date been an export-oriented activity and has generated little in the way of secondary economic activity. History, therefore, contradicts this report's claim that sustained, long-term benefits will accrue to northerners.
The report also recommends, and I quote:
Economic development of the north must proceed with full recognition of the legitimate interests of northern people and the protection of the environment.
Yet, in several places the report states that mineral rights should remain vested in the Crown regardless of future agreements with native people. This idea makes one wonder just what the committee considers to be legitimate interests.
While saying on the one hand that industry wishes to protect the environment, the report questions the continuing validity of the Thelon Game Sanctuary, a region which the uranium mining industry wishes to explore. The report also recommends that if economic development is to be prohibited on certain lands, the area of these lands should be kept to a minimum and that selection of lands take into account their potential mineral value. This seems to say that land set aside for environmental protection should be located where there are no minerals rather than where there are important wildlife populations or environmentally sensitive features to be protected.
If mining is to make a positive contribution to the long-term development of the north, I feel that it must be taken in its proper perspective as only one of several elements which can contribute to the benefit of northerners. It must not, for example, be allowed to interfere with management of renewable resources which are essential to the continuing survival of northern culture and economic well-being. Above all, the mining industry must not be permitted to supersede the legitimate rights and aspirations of the people of the north.

In the Speech from the Throne reference was made to the diversity of Canada as a national asset, and yet the thrust of northern policy seems to offer the native people only one alternative, that of assimilation. The throne speech

October 16, 1979
The Address-Mr. Ittinuar
made no reference to the Inuit or to the constitution, it made no reference to political development in the Northwest Territories, and in fact if recent developments in the Yukon are any indication, the present government is not really interested in involving native people in political change, except in a token way after the fact.
During the election campaign the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) promised to let Yukoners decide through a referendum the question of provincial status. However, last week the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development took steps which bring the Yukon Territory government dangerously close in form to provincehood, and there was no referendum before that. I say "dangerously" for two reasons. First of all, the move was made without prior consultation with the Council of Yukon Indians whose outstanding claims are susceptible to the whims of politicians and political moods, and perhaps I should include myself in that circle. Secondly, with the framework of a provincial government already in place, the question of a referendum becomes academic. Residents of the Northwest Territories and Yukoners alike may, and do, desire responsible government, but we feel very strongly about being a part of the democratic planning process of such a government.
In the search for solutions to the question of political development in the north, the logical place to look is in the aspirations of the population itself. We believe this is the democratic way. The aspirations of the people in this case are embodied in the desire for a new province named Nunavut. This desire has been well thought out. It divides the Northwest Territories into manageable proportions, each of which has enough homogeneity to make public administration more efficient. The summary report of the advisory commission on the development of government in the Northwest Territories in 1966 recommended that Yellowknife be made the capital of the Northwest Territories. I wish to quote one of the reasons given. It reads as follows:
It would be an appropriate location for the present political unit of the Northwest Territories or for the western part of a divided territory.
The Government of Canada, in creating the constituency of Nunatsiaq, has already recognized the natural boundary separating the eastern and western halves. Nunatsiaq is a culturally and geographically distinct area north of the tree line.
I now call upon the Government of Canada to recognize the legitimate aspirations of the people of Nunavut to become equal participants in the Canadian confederation. These aspirations are not in the least radical. It was only 30 years ago that Newfoundland joined confederation. At a time when national unity is being tried and tested, the people of Nunavut wish to be welcomed by their fellow Canadians into the fold of confederation.
On principle, I should like to speak in Inuktitut and say-

Mr. Speaker, 1 want to take this opportunity to extend to you personally my warmest greetings, as a friend and as one who can do an excellent job and assume his new responsibilities. 1 also want to take this opportunity to thank the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) and the entire cabinet for the trust they have put in me. It is a great honour for me and for my constituents that I should be a member of the cabinet. Mr. Speaker, I hope to live up to the expectations and to serve the best interests of my country.
I also want to take the time to commend the Speaker of the House on his appointment to the office he has served with such excellence thus far and where he has shown his characteristic wisdom. I therefore want to wish him all the success he deserves and I might add that I truthfully would not want to be in his place, especially when he must give certain rulings. By the same token, I would not want to leave unmentioned the motion of the co-movers of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, two newcomers to this House who join us for this Thirty-first Parliament. That reminds me, Mr. Speaker, of my first years or first days in the House of Commons, some 12 years ago. I also want to congratulate all members on their reelection, in some cases, or their election, in other cases, especially the right hon. Prime Minister who, in less than three years, rose from private member to leader of his party to first citizen of Canada. It is a great honour for me and I think it should be felt by all Canadians.
Finally, I should like also to congratulate the new opposition leader (Mr. Trudeau), the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) and the Leader of the Social Credit Party of Canada (Mr. Roy) and wish them too the best of luck. I should like to spend a few minutes, Mr. Speaker, to thank especially the people of my constituency of Joliette for sending me for the fourth time as their elected representative in the House of Commons. I am aware that this is a great honour and I have every intention of living up to their expectations. 1 have always been faithful to them, Mr. Speaker, in spite of difficult circumstances. I have always held the mandate received from my constituents as something extremely precious, and I feel that their testimony has still more significance because the right hon. Prime Minister has now asked me to be part of his cabinet. Mr. Speaker, this is an honour I share with all my constituents.
I have been sitting in the House of Commons since 1968 and I have made it my duty to be sensitive to the needs of the electors in my riding. Despite the new responsibilities entrusted to me as Minister of Supply and Services, I shall certainly not neglect my own riding; I shall see to it that my
October 16, 1979

electors benefit from some economic fall-out. I represent a riding that is in need of a new impetus in the economic field, and as the representative of the riding of Joliette in the House of Commons, 1 intend to spare no effort in helping to set the economy of my area back on track, as well as that of the whole country, which is not incompatible with renewed economic activity in my own area.
My electors have been patient. Some will recognize that. They have waited almost 12 years to be represented in cabinet.
1 certainly have no intention of disappointing them on that score, Mr. Speaker; I shall participate more than ever in consultations and the implementation of programs designed to improve the quality of life. Mr, Speaker, I would also like to take a few minutes to explain briefly the responsibilities of my department. My department, I am sure, as well as most public organizations responsible for purchases have always endeavoured to obtain the best value at the best price in deals concluded on behalf of the government.
The federal government has long since recognized that its purchase policy could promote economic development in Canada. Several provinces have acted likewise, each in its own way. Current financial conditions require that we grant more importance to our purchases to stimulate the Canadian economy and 1 would like to deal briefly with this matter. The public organizations responsible for business play an important role in the economy. In recent years, for example, the Department of Supply and Services has purchased goods and services worth annually some $3 billion. It is a substantial amount which represents only 15 per cent of the $20 billion spent annually at all levels of government for the purchase of goods and services.
We must not underestimate the economic repercussions of these expenses. Of course, governments are becoming ever more conscious of the fact that they have to exert the economic influence they have as buyers of goods and services, but it is also obvious that in order to obtain maximum advantages for Canada as a whole and for every province, we have devised a more co-operative working scheme with a view to making our buyer status more widely known.
No government or department can permanently play a pioneering role in that field. Which brings us down to the fundamental question, namely how to achieve unanimity among governments to rationalize and integrate our activities as much as is necessary. We have to achieve that unanimity within the limits of our objectives of integrity and profitability. Moreover, my department's policy is to give preference to companies whose head office is in Canada provided that the competition is sufficiently strong to assure us we will get our money's worth when time comes to negotiate contracts. The effect of that policy is to give Canadian enterprises more than 80 per cent of the total value of the market the Department of Supply and Services represents. As for the rest of our purchases from foreign companies, which represent 20 per cent of
The Address-Mr. La Salle
all our purchases, they generally concern military equipment which is of great technical complexity and which is not produced in Canada. The federal government tries to pull out of these purchases beneficial repercussions on the Canadian economy.
That is done by subcontracting and through the investments of suppliers in Canada. With respect to regional purchases, the policy of my department requires that goods and services be bought in the region involved provided there is enough competition. Consequently about 30 per cent of the purchases of my department are made through regional offices located all over Canada. As to the remaining 70 per cent, my department tries to make sure that all qualified Canadian corporations are invited to tender. The federal policy requires that certain products, like textile products, clothing and ships, be purchased exclusively in Canada. In addition, the scientific and technical products acquisition policy as well as the policy dealing with ammunitions give preference to Canadian corporations.
My department has tried to promote the interest of small and medium businesses. On average, it has given some 71 per cent of the number and 40 per cent of the annual value of those deals, worth $585 million, to small businesses. This percentage compares favourably with the over-all contribution of small businesses to the Canadian economy which is estimated to be between 25 and 30 per cent of the gross national product. This brief outline of the accomplishments of my department shows that worth-while efforts have been made to help Canadian industry but I believe we can still do much more.
In this respect, 1 believe it would be appropriate to rely more heavily on certain initiatives to get the most for our money while at the same time seeking to increase our help to Canadian industry through closer co-operation between three heavily involved departments, namely the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and my department. 1 believe we could consider in future studies on ways to make ourselves certain products we have to buy abroad which would enable us, along with those two other departments, to attract those industries to those so-called soft areas where unemployment is high. As I see it, perhaps that would dispel the concern voiced by the premier of Quebec last night in Hull, since he aims at establishing equity of purchases proportionally to the population of the provinces. Mr. Speaker, I am committed to try to meet this objective with the co-operation of these two departments so that my province may finally be treated equally and so that the purchases may be made throughout the country with the same equity, with which all hon. members on the other side as well as my colleagues would certainly agree.

October 16, 1979
The Address-Mr. La Salle
If you will allow me, Mr. Speaker, I shall take this opportunity to express my personal satisfaction at the fact that the Speech from the Throne refers to certain measures aimed at stimulating the Canadian economy.
In my capacity of a member of the cabinet, I insisted as early as the Jasper meeting that some emphasis be placed on economic revival, and I am pleased to see that my message was understood. The reinforcement of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, the original program, it must be recognized, of tax credits for mortgage interests and property taxes, the development of a national tourist industry development strategy in cooperation with provinces, assistance for small and medium businessess, Mr. Speaker, these are all clear indications of the will of our government to take direct action to put the Canadian economy back on its feet. And 1 would not want to forget to mention the intention of the government to establish a national assistance program for the handicapped.
Our decision to hold a national conference on economic development with all our partners, that is business, unions, co-operatives and other groups in all the provinces, shows that we intend to consult those involved before deciding on any course of action. This conference, which is a sort of summit meeting of all economic development officers in Canada, reflects the new spirit of co-operation that the right hon. Prime Minister wants to instill in our country.
In this regard, I would like to underline, like the right hon. Prime Minister, that it is no longer a few members of the elite who decide on the direction to give the policies of Canada, but members of parliament elected democratically and representing all the provinces. This is a good illustration, Mr. Speaker, of true federalism which goes from the bottom up instead of what we have suffered for too long, a federalism shaped like an inverted pyramid which suffocates any private initiative. I am also happy to note the open mind with which we intend to conduct federal-provincial relations. This will be our trademark, Mr. Speaker, and not only until the Quebec referendum, but also afterwards.
Personally I have always spoken openly in favour of a renewed and decentralized form of federalism. It is not without regret that I have witnessed for the past ten years this battle waged by the commandos of the former minister in charge of federal-provincial relations and which has only resulted in hardening the positions taken by the provinces, Quebec in particular, toward the federal government. I therefore rejoice at the announcement made by the Prime Minister with regard to this matter wherein he urged all members of the House to adopt a more open minded stance, more directly geared to economic realities and our differences which should be better understood in order to better unite us. This spirit of co-operation pleases me and I for one certainly intend to put it into practice openly, Mr. Speaker. I would like to add right now that in my case this is not a sudden conversion to a new
style because it has been a point of view that I have held ever since I started representing my riding in this House.
However, I understand that the attitude suggested to us by the Prime Minister will not be easy for everyone. Nevertheless I think that the time has come to bury the hatchet. From now on, we shall see the start of a new era. It is the end of fruitless battles, the disappearance of scarecrows that were used to frighten everyone. It is also the end of propaganda. Everything has been said and it is now time for action.
Since May 22, the date of the election of our party, an easing of minds has replaced the stress maintained for too long and deliberately created by our opponents. In the last four months we have tried to emphasize the aspects which draw us closer to the provinces, particularly Quebec, rather than underlining points of divergence. I really believe that we shall have to develop the approach which consists of listening to the desires of other people.
Mr. Speaker, we have witnessed for too long a dialogue of the deaf between the federal government and my province in particular. I think we are going towards more openness. We live in a tremendously rich country with considerable wealth. It will be to our advantage to share all we have at a time when the economic situation invites us to think of our fellow citizens.
The government of which I have the privilege to be a member refused to choose national unity as its platform in the last election and I am happy it did. In fact, on this side of the House, we believe that there are many other priorities requiring immediate intervention and if the re-establishment of an economic climate is achieved, we should not neglect the importance of constitutional changes that would be much easier in a climate more favourable to discussions and negotiations with the provinces.
I have always considered that it would not be very advantageous to create a confrontation with partners which form the Canadian nation. But I still believe we have everything to gain by finding together, in a spontaneous research effort, better ways of living where all Canadians, French and English alike, will live in unison.
Mr. Speaker, our opponents too often demonstrated that a common ground will not be found by accusing others, especially not our Quebec partners. More flexibility, some open-mindedness, less arrogance and intolerance seem to be called for if we are to start on the road to reconciliation, especially on the eve of the forthcoming Quebec referendum to be held next spring.
I noticed that some hon. members opposite were outraged last week-they may still be today-that we put aside what I would call an instrument of confrontation and aggression, the referendum bill, which I fought vigorously last spring. Our party, our government also realized this was not the way to treat people in Quebec. We believe in the maturity of Quebeckers. We are confident that, with proposals and above all

October 16, 1979

with an attitude of concertation rather than confrontation, we will prove to all Quebeckers that their future and the numerous benefits offered by this country still lie within a constitutional framework, albeit much more flexible that anything we could invent until now. Therefore, when 1 listened to the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Deniger), who earlier raised questions:
How come Ontario and British Columbia pay more for goods when they could get them cheaper in Quebec? How come our economy is almost at its lowest? How come this country is divided? I forgive him, Mr. Speaker, he is a new member. He may not have followed what his party did in the last ten years. How is it that a government made up of about 60 Quebeckers that has ruled for 16 years has put the country in a situation like this? How is it that they have been unable to provide Quebeckers with the message they were expecting?
How about the co-operation Quebeckers expected from them? The member should know that the number of people in Quebec dissatisfied with federalism as advocated by his party has increased 1 do not know how many times. They have failed and they should ask themselves how it is that our country is in such a poor economic state. How come his own party has let unemployment soar from 200,000 to 1,500,000 in less than ten years? That is the kind of questions the member for Longueuil (Mr. Olivier) should ask himself instead of interrupting those who have points to make like me today.
I suggest that this adaptability on our part and, as I said, our willingness to listen to our counterparts in the various provinces will greatly help us build the foundation of a rejuvenated federalism much more in line with the provinces' aspirations. 1 am not inventing anything, Mr. Speaker, simply watching what is going on in Canada. Over the past 12 years which 1 have spent sitting in the House as elected representative for the Joliette riding, I have witnessed a great many confrontations which could have been prevented, in my opinion, if only the previous administration had demonstrated greater understanding.
Need 1 remind my hon. colleagues, for instance, of the sales tax imbroglio when 1 was deeply ashamed to hear my Quebec colleagues fly in the face of the most evident aspirations and interests of the province of Quebec. These are the people who are now accusing us of selling out to the provinces. Yet, they are the very people who are responsible for Canadian unity being put to the test, because they enjoyed these confrontations with the provinces; now they are wondering what essentially we mean when we talk about a greater need for understanding and adaptability with the provinces.
This desire to allow the provinces to participate in the major national decisions, this deep desire on the part of the Prime Minister and all my cabinet colleagues to give the provinces the opportunity to discuss important decisions having direct
The Address-Mr. La Salle
implications on their own economy: here is the kind of federalism and the kind of administration we want to establish, Mr. Speaker. They charge that we are willing to sell out to the provinces and yet they are the ones who, after 16 years in power, have succeeded in tearing the country apart as is the case today, Mr. Speaker. I feel no sympathy for that kind of argument which they use too often.
Even the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Pepin), last week in Winnipeg together with a few Liberals, of course, are looking for a side track, a more secure way. 1 understand them because 1 have gone through that myself if it can make you feel better. In another connection, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say two words about a daily concern, namely that of the development of agriculture in Canada and in Quebec in particular. Let no one worry about that. In this House I represent a riding whose economy, for the major part agricultural, depends on the resources of the soil. My riding of Joliette is an area whose production is largely agricultural in nature.
The situation of the dairy industry as a whole is also of major concern to us. It has experienced difficult years. My hon. friends across the way will remember that. We were not in power, Mr. Speaker, but 1 remember well what happened. I merely want to point out, for the guidance of my colleagues, that the Progressive Conservative government authorized, within a few weeks after May 22, an increase in the quotas of milk produced for export by some three million hundred weights, which represents sales of some $39 million for dairy producers. In the near future we also expect to increase by 1 to 2 per cent the quotas of milk and its by-products for consumption. The 20 cents previously withheld and recently reimbursed to the producers amounted to $26 million of which $13 million went to Quebec alone. To my mind, those figures prove our consideration for agriculture. Last month, my colleague, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), had the opportunity of inaugurating a processing plant at Sainte-Claire; the project had been initiated by the previous government. I am very happy to say the plant opened recently.
That was part of an investment amounting to $2 million which also allowed the Department of Regional Economic

Expansion to spend $500,000 in the port of Quebec to store about 100,000 tons of products. That will bring into the economy of the greater Quebec City area investments amounting to $50 million. I think, Mr. Speaker, my time is running out. I wanted to take this opportunity to remind the House that we are looking forward to an excellent session, and that we also expect to achieve certain objectives, including two which are fundamental: restoring the economic climate in this country, and of course decreasing unemployment with, hopefully, some help insofar as one would want to be objective enough. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I join in congratulating you upon your appointment to your high office. I share also in the tradition of this House in congratulating the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) and the hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. MacDonald) upon their speeches. Perhaps I may be permitted a personal note of congratulations to the hon. member for Cardigan, since I suppose in a way he is my member of parliament, representing as he does a beautiful area where 1 am happy to say I still have the land on which my ancestors settled some 200 years ago.
Mr. Speaker, I represent a new constituency in metropolitan Toronto, Etobicoke North, a vital area where industry, particularly light and high-technology industry, leads our constituents to take a lively interest in economic policies pursued by the government, particularly those relating to industrial stategy. Etobicoke North is a constituency of hard-working, diligent citizens, many of whom have only recently become

October 16, 1979

Canadians, and all of whom are eager to see new opportunities created for Canadians to participate in the development of their own country, to realize their pride in Canadian initiative and capacities.
It is partly for that reason, Mr. Speaker, that I wish to say something this afternoon about trade and industrial development in Canada and about our assistance to developing countries.
The GATT agreements, completed last spring in Geneva, are the most recent stage in the long, difficult progress toward freer trade which began in the late 1930s. The recent so-called Tokyo Round was in several respects the most demanding in that prolonged process. The easier tariff reductions had been made as the result of the earlier negotiations; by 1973, when the Tokyo discussions began, the ingenuity of man had devised such a panoply of non-tariff barriers to replace traditional tariffs that growth in international trade was becoming increasingly trammelled.
Against this background, it is remarkable that so much was accomplished in Geneva. Much more, however, remains to be done here at home if Canada is to benefit fully from these marathon trade talks. Much of the task remaining concerns our relations with the United States. I take as my starting point certain implications for Canada from the GATT agreements, but Canadians should be under no illusion that we really have before us a much more fundamental question: our ability to order our future economic relations with the United States so that we can pursue our own unique social and cultural needs-so that, in short, we can give greater expression to our Canadian values, practices and traditions.
Canada and the United States are now committed to virtual free trade at the end of eight years, in the broader context of global reductions in tariff and non-tariff barriers. This is a development which, at least in theory, is to be welcomed.Freer access to world markets, and freer access to one of the largest and most prosperous of such markets, the United States of America, should help Canadian industry to rid itself of that persistent deterrent to greater productivity and international competitiveness: the hitherto limited size of the market for Canadian products.
The question of the actual costs and benefits of freer trade is a complex one, Mr. Speaker, but it is now one which requires prompt attention. In the past, the discussion has been a somewhat leisurely one; with the conclusion of the GATT agreements, it becomes an urgent one. If my advocacy of early action appears to have any partisan overtone, I should like to draw the government's attention to a recent plea from Mr. Robert Stanfield. In April he stated:
In view of the importance of economies of scale, can we continue to thrive without a wider area of free trade with the United States? On the other hand, can we preserve sufficient independence if we do have a wider area of free trade with the United States? The question of entering the European Common Market was a difficult one for the United Kingdom, but no one country dominates the Common Market as the United States would dominate any partial or total common market between Canada and the United States.
The Address-Mr. MacLaren
Mr. Stanfield went on to say:
These questions are crucially important to Canada and to Canadian politicians ... However, there has been little political debate yet about such a move ... It will be interesting to see whether Canadians try to halt further economic integration with the U.S. and accept the resulting economic difficulties, or on the other hand try to secure increased access to the U.S. market and to build in the necessary safeguards. The debate must soon begin in earnest, and at the highest level of Canadian politics.
1 have noted some theoretical benefits of free trade. Reality is, unfortunately, somewhat different from economic theory. Canada is unique among non-communist nations in that the country to which 70 per cent of our trade, including 82 per cent of our manufactured exports, is directed, is the same country that controls a majority of our manufacturing sector and significant segments of our resources and related industries. The uniqueness of this Canadian situation is underlined if one recalls that, in the post-war European experience of free trade, there has been, as one observer has noted, "the union of more equally sized industrial economies and/or ones whose industry is not dominated economically by the branches of one neighbour."
Today United States corporations dominate manufacturing in Canada despite tariff walls. Tomorrow we shall have virtually no tariff walls or non-tariff barriers with the U.S.A.
The extent of foreign investment in Canada, mainly from the United States, is familiar. In any assessment of the net benefits and debits of this investment, it must be recognized that this has brought in its train a degree of foreign indebtedness again unique among industrialized nations. During recent decades there has been an increasingly large outflow of royalties and dividends and a parallel perceived need to keep Canadian interest rates above those in the U.S.A., with all the implications that this has for our own fiscal policy.
Second, given the fact that the United States is both our major trading partner and controls significant sectors of our economy, much of what is described as "trade" between our two countries is, in fact, intra-company movements of components or finished products within a single U.S. corporation, not deals at arm's length and not necessarily governed by market forces.
Third, with regard to exports, while some subsidiaries in Canada have received "global mandates" for their products, others are either assigned restricted export territories or excluded altogether from exporting. As an additional method of achieving greater profitability for the parent corporation, limitations are also in many cases placed on research and development, product development, or manufacturing diversification.
I was interested to note that, in a recent speech, the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Wilson) deplored, as he should, the lack of export freedom of some subsidiaries in Canada. I regretted however, that he was silent about what should be done. A report recently made to his colleague, the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Grafftey), by the ad hoc advisory committee on research and develop-
254

October 16, 1979
The Address-Mr. MacLaren
merit sets out a promising review process with subsidiaries restricted in their export freedom. 1 recommend that the Minister for State for International Trade read that report. There will, I hope, be opportunities to pursue this point at a later stage.
Against this background, it would be idle, in light of the recent GATT agreements, to regard tariff or non-tariff barriers as being effective tools in any long-term industrial strategy for Canada. To achieve our dual goals of greater industrial development and Canadian control, we must look elsewhere. In selecting our tools, first let us attempt to visualize what the principal adverse effects of free trade with the United States may be.
As the possibilities for increased profits resulting from free trade are fully recognized by U.S. corporations, presumably they will review which manufacturing subsidiaries in Canada might be profitably shut down and moved to a U.S. factory, in a continental rationalization to achieve greater productivity, including economies of scale. The size of U.S. investment in Canada would be no blanket deterrent to such a trend, although transport and other costs might be in some cases. The current migration of certain U.S. manufacturing activities from New England to the lower cost southern states readily suggets the mobility of such investment.
Further, as both Canada and the United States increasingly feel the impact of higher energy costs and especially the competition of low-cost manufactures from the Third World, bringing heavy pressure on labour-intensive manufacturing, presumably the first jobs to be preserved by U.S. corporations would be at home rather than in Canada, whenever such a choice had to be made. Finally, even if a branch plant is left in Canada, it would become fully integrated into a continental operation, reducing the need for senior management talent in Canada.
While this migration was occurring, Canadian firms presumably would concurrently attempt to take advantage of free entry into the U.S. market and overseas. Although the U.S. reaction to free trade which I have described is likely to be successful for the corporations involved, since it would accord with the simple laws of the marketplace, it is not at all as certain that Canadian initiatives to benefit from free trade will be equally successful. Indeed, multinational corporations are, by their very nature, more likely to have the resources and flexibility required to take full advantage of the opportunities offered by free trade. It would, for example, be a reasonable, if broad, assumption that, unless adjustment assistance, including assistance in meeting capital costs in reorganization, were provided to small Canadian firms, they will be decidedly less likely to make the transition to free trade than a major U.S. corporation already familiar with both the U.S. and Canadian markets.
Given the fact that significant sectors of the Canadian economy are dominated by U.S. corporations, the Canadian government will be the only entity large enough to take a lead in attempting to select industrial sectors capable of competing in international markets, especially in the United States.

Although governments, with the possible exception of the Japanese, do not seem to be very good at foreseeing the industrial future or predicting the course of technological change, and although it would be an uphill struggle against dominant U.S. corporations, the Canadian government should attempt to foster the emergence of viable Canadian players in the U.S. economy and beyond.
The necessary industrial development policy to achieve this will be found in several respects synonymous with a policy promoting investment by Canadians in Canadian companies or the acquisition of foreign-controlled subsidiaries.
The creation of the Foreign Investment Review Agency resulted from the growing realization on the part of the federal government of the day that ad hoc measures to deal with foreign investment were inadequate and that more was necessary to meet public concern over the disadvantages from the growing foreign investment in Canada.
It may be that FIRA has increased the benefits to Canada of such investment, but the fact remains that through both reinvestment and acquisition foreign control has continued to grow. I for one regret that the governments of Canada since the Second World War have found themselves incapable of doing more to ensure benefits to Canadians from foreign investment and to promote investment by Canadians in Canada.
The previous government did put into place several policies aimed mainly at promoting Canadian entrepreneurship in small and medium-sized businesses, a sector not so dominated by foreign corporations. These policies have contributed in varying degrees to the recent growth in new Canadian businesses, the more rapid growth of existing ones and the acquisition of foreign-controlled firms. They also represent the degree to which both the federal and provincial governments have already intervened in substantial ways to assist the private sector in dealing with structural problems, particularly in the manufacturing sector.
However, an overly interventionist approach on the part of government may well lead to greater inefficiencies and have little real effect on productivity. There is a vast difference between policies such as free trade, both internal and external, a more effective competition policy, particularly on mergers and monopolies and tax incentives, on the one hand, and government procurement policy, enforced mergers, and protection against imports of technology on the other.
The government should define a role for itself that encourages, without interfering unduly in the private sector; that promotes co-ordination between levels of government and among industries; that builds a positive relationship with business and labour and supports a nationally based industrial strategy emphasizing employment opportunities and Canadian ownership.
For some years now, the phrase "industrial strategy" has been much in vogue. At its most simplistic, the strategy has been put in military terms: a grand plan which, if once devised and followed consistently, would surely lead to victory. In
October 16, 1979

these terms, the search for an industrial strategy has been as barren as the search for the Holy Grail.
There cannot, in fact, be such a thing as a single, grand industrial strategy. Residual tariff protection may, for example, remain important for some sectors and the very last thing that other sectors require. Recognition of the fact that for Canada there cannot be a single strategy but rather a number of co-ordinated sector strategies led the previous government to establish the Board of Economic Development. It in turn worked with labour, business and the provincial governments to begin the elaboration of 21 sector strategies.
We must continue to develop more specific sector policies and instruments. We must begin to categorize our industrial activity according to the potential that it offers this country in the immediate and longer term. Those industries and sectors which have high potential for producing internationally competitive goods should receive priority in industrial incentives.
Other sectors of the Canadian economy are in need of adjustment assistance to meet the challenge of increasing imports, particularly from the Third World. Any sector strategies worthy of the name will necessarily raise questions of investment priorities of both Canadian and foreign-controlled corporations in Canada and the incentives of both the federal and provincial governments to encourage them in certain agreed directions. The provinces have, for example, significant powers regarding mergers and acquisitions; their full participation will be essential.
Within this framework of a co-ordinated industrial sector strategy, the role of FIRA would be enhanced. It could then realize its potential as a tool of industrial strategy. If the federal government, in consultation with other major players in the economy, were able to develop genuine, as opposed to self-serving, industrial strategies for major sectors, a foreign takeover or expansion could be judged by FIRA on the criteria of its compatability with designated internationally competitive sectors, and industries within those sectors. 1 am pleased that in a special committee of this House there will be opportunity to develop additional thinking about foreign investment, including FIRA. 1 am sure that the committee will be ably chaired by the hon. member for Mississauga North (Mr. Jupp).
I have said that additional measures are required to promote Canadian ownership, an essential development if we are to achieve that degree of economic independence necessary to enable us to pursue our own fiscal needs and to reduce the unacceptably high outflow of dividends, royalties and other invisibles which so bedevils our attempts at responsible economic management. There will, I understand, be occasion during the budget debate and when the GATT agreements are placed before this House to advance proposals in detail. Accordingly, I shall merely touch upon a few today.
Although tax measures can sometimes be rightly attacked as socially inequitable, they can, if implemented wisely, be an effective means of encouraging Canadians to invest in Canadi-
The Address-Mr. MacLaren
an equities. Tax shelter provisions have directed considerable amounts of additional investment into specific areas. There appears to be no reason why this tool should not be applied, as appropriate, to Canadian-controlled ventures in other sectors.
The establishment of business credit insurance companies, as proposed by the Board of Economic Development, should help to open additional major pools of capital, including pension funds.
With regard to the vital area of research and development, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association has rightly urged tax incentives to make such investment more attractive in comparison with other investment opportunities. Share ownership by employees and additional activities for the Canada Development Corporation offer further opportunities to promote Canadian ownership and to assist Canadian companies in equipping themselves for the formidable challenges facing Canada as we enter a world of freer trade.
These are but a few instances where progress can be made in encouraging Canadian investment in Canada. There will be occasion to develop this thinking further. But if Canadian exports and ownership of our own industry are to be successfully extended, with all the attendant benefits for Canadians, three fundamental steps must be taken without delay. First, the establishment of a consultative forum involving business, labour and federal and provincial governments is long overdue. Second, federal efforts must be intensified to reduce regional preoccupations and to promote a freer internal market in Canada. Third, agreement must be reached soon with the United States on the terms of mutually beneficial government purchasing and on limiting the use of countervailing duties.
As Canada adjusts to free trade with the United States over the next eight years, the implementation of a comprehensive industrial strategy should help to put us in a position to compete more effectively in the U.S. market, as well as with U.S. imports at home, and to encourage Canadian ownership. In this evolving trade situation, there are both new opportunities and new challenges for Canadians. But we should also recognize that there are limitations arising from historical trends and certain geographic factors which will determine the scope and nature of those opportunities and challenges.
So it is, Mr. Speaker, in the yet broader area of Canada's external relations of which trade relations are such an important part. It was both a surprise and a cause of regret that while the throne speech raised several issues with a foreign affairs dimension-for example, oil pricing-there is not one word about Canada's foreign policy in either the throne speech or in the Prime Minister's (Mr. Clark) subsequent speech in this debate. Not a word about our relations with the United States, NATO, the United Nations, the commonwealth and la Francophonie, peacekeeping, disarmament, development assistance. Not one word, yet paradoxically during the many months which passed between the calling of the election and the calling of Parliament, it was foreign affairs which absorbed much of the time of the Prime Minister. The Tokyo economic summit, the Commonwealth conference in Zambia and the profound silliness of souring our hitherto good and growing

October 16, 1979
The Address-Mr. MacLaren
relations with the Moslem world were issues to which the new government devoted much of its first months in office. And yet in the throne speech, not one word about foreign policy.
After more than four months Canadians have little more information on the approach of the new government toward our foreign relations than the two recent speeches of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Miss MacDonald), one at the United Nations and the second in Toronto. Additional clues, albeit vague and contradictory, may be gleaned from the speeches of other ministers.
Given the confusing character of these various statements, there is ample opportunity to speculate about how the government intends to contribute to international peace, disarmament and prosperity. Time, however, is limited, so 1 shall restrict myself to the questions of development assistance and, by implication, our relations with the Third World.
Since coming to office, the minister has stated that government policy is to concentrate Canadian aid on those countries approaching what several decades ago became known as economic "take-off", or self-sustaining growth. What is one to make of this curious statement? For example, if one does oneself what one would have others do, who then would remain to assist the poorest of the poor countries? To take another instance, is one to assume that Canada in a search for "takeoff' countries will now direct its aid to the OPEC countries, countries which are achieving capital inflows adequate, if wisely employed, to ensure "take-off'?
If it is now the minister's intention to attempt to accelerate their "take-off' process by directing our aid toward the OPEC countries, she may be disappointed in her ambitions. Many of these countries are the same which have been alienated by the government's gratuitous and hapless intrusion into the long-vexed question of Jerusalem. The minister must accordingly look to other regions for those more affluent developing countries where Canada is to concentrate its aid, perhaps Latin America. Yet the minister's recently stated misgivings about human rights in Argentina and the consequent deplorable failure to develop our trade relations there would seem to exclude Argentina. Many of the other Latin American countries, such as Brazil and Venezuela, are rich in resources; can she really have them in mind? On the other hand, few countries of Africa have yet achieved the circumstances attending economic "take-off', so presumably they do not qualify. In any case, Africa is excluded, since the minister stated in Toronto that Africa is no longer an area of commitment for Canada. The fact is that southern Africa, especially Namibia, represents one of the most inflammable areas of the world today, but the minister asked in her Toronto speech, who cares?
One more example: Pakistan, a country singled out for having said some things which, in the minister's view, were unfriendly. Now our assistance to Pakistan is brought into question. Here indeed is a new doctrine for Canadian aid: "You will receive aid only if you agree with us, with our policies, even if Canadians themselves consider them to be singularly wrong-headed".

I have spent a few minutes on this review of recent bizarre statements on development assistance by the minister because their cumulative effect has been to spread confusion. Our links with many developing countries have their roots in shared history. The countries of formerly British Asia and Africa are tied to us through a common link with Britain, which has become an enduring connection through the institutions of the commonwealth. Our relations with French-speaking Africa are made closer by our shared membership in la Francophonie. These are not ties to be dismissed lightly, as they have been by the minister.
We maintain these connections with the Third World for reasons that have as much to do with international stability and security as with international charity. We cannot therefore dismiss countries because they are not about to "take off' economically. While many of the poorest countries are not yet in a position to offer commercial opportunities to Canadians, our assistance is not therefore wasted. In our volatile world, links between developed and developing countries play a stabilizing role. The intense north-south debate of the past few years should at least have taught us that developing countries are more articulate and more united than ever before, and that their participation as members on a more even footing in the international economic system is essential if we are to be able to preserve a mutually advantageous equilibrium.
We cannot afford at this point in north-south relations to be parsimonious and unimaginative. Even the poorest developing countries have an equal voice at international gatherings. And their comparatively more wealthy allies, countries such as Mexico, Nigeria and Indonesia, have been supporting their demands. Can it really be to Canada's benefit, 1 ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs, to cut off the ties which have been laboriously built up over time in the hope of obtaining some undefined and possibly unrealizable benefits for Canadian exporters?
We must continue to act upon the principles that underlie our involvement in peace keeping and development assistance around the world. Canada's contributions to world peace and more harmonious relations between north and south may be quantitatively small, but they continue to have an impact as evidence of our willingness as a prosperous nation to contribute to the advancement of others. We must not reduce foreign policy to a daily or monthly balance sheet. Our contributions, whether in the form of peace keeping troops or development projects, do not necessarily result in immediately tangible rewards. Yet we are undoubtedly contributing to security and economic growth on a global scale.
Let us have done with cant and compounded contradictions. Let us again, drawing upon our Judaeo-Christian traditions, drawing upon the skills and knowledge of our commonwealth and Francophone background, continue the task which all the governments of post-war Canada have set themselves. Let us continue to demonstrate the imagination and perseverance
October 16, 1979

which has marked Canada's approach to external aid throughout the past decades.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my distinct privilege to be present in this House today. I am proud to be the member for Scarborough Centre. I am here with humility, remembering that my presence in this chamber is the end result of the support of many good people in Scarborough Centre whose judgment it was that I should be their voice in Parliament. It is my responsibility, Mr. Speaker, to work hard for them six full days of each and every week. I do so with great joy. On the seventh day, I rest and recharge my batteries to renew myself mentally, physically and spiritually. Then, too, the seventh day I spend with my family, with our three boys of whom we are very proud, and with my husband.
With your permission, sir, 1 will pay tribute to my husband. It was he, when I was asked to consider declaring as a candidate for nomination, who acknowledged that the time was right for me, on behalf of our family, to offer our community of Scarborough Centre the ultimate service one can give: to serve as a member of Parliament. It was he who added his strength to mine during the extended and indefinite pre-writ period. It was he, with his superb sense of humour, who kept me and those around me from losing a sense of perspective during the election campaign. And now, Mr. Speaker, it is he who willingly fulfils the role of parliamentary spouse concurrently with that of husband.

Tribute, too, should be paid to you, Mr. Speaker. Congratulations have been extended to you by other members here. I add mine, combined with tribute, because it is fitting to do so to one who has displayed such reason, moderation and wisdom while exercising his duties. Congratulations are also due to the Clerk of the House. He comes from Saskatchewan, the province of my birth, so I feel a particular warmth as I extend best wishes to him and to his colleagues at the outset of the Thirty-first Parliament.
Mr. Speaker, I stand in this august chamber eager to participate in this session of Parliament, clothed in the innocence of a neophyte. I aspired to come here for many reasons, the main motive being to represent the people of Scarborough Centre. During the campaign 1 was asked what class of people reside in my constituency. My reply was: "The salt of the earth class." We are ordinary folk, Mr. Speaker, the kind of folk who built this great land. We live in town houses, bungalows, apartments; we have churches and schools; we are young, middle aged and elderly; we are small business and light industry; we are right in the centre of Scarborough. We are the hub of Scarborough. I was eager to represent these people because I could see at the time that the administration-now the former administration-was intent on eliminating the middle class, eradicating it from Canada. My concern was acute because a thriving middle class is one of the main elements of democracy.
The Address-Mrs. Stratas
And 1 sought to come to this august chamber, Mr. Speaker, because in my former life-my pre-political life-1 had known the frustration of being mute. So I sought to come here to speak for those who were mute, to speak for the poor, to speak for the young, to speak for those who wish me to speak for them, to speak for the ordinary folks. The Master Maker exercised His creative genius best when he made us, the ordinary folks. That is why he made so many of us.
He made us all so different, yet the more we are different the more we are alike. We have the same pain, fear, joy and hope. We have the capacity, when necessity demands it, to change from ordinary folk and become extraordinary folk, to rise to a challenge and overcome adversity. Above all, we have the same innocence, and it is this innocence which makes us shy away from something we know little about.
Thus, I was delighted to hear in the Speech from the Throne which His Excellency delivered last week that freedom of information was the first of what 1 call pillars of progress to be contained in the speech. Citizens and Parliament can control government if information is public, and citizens can come to know government. For our own sakes we must know government, and then and only then will the erosion of democracy be curtailed.
I come here as an idealist. Someone once defined an idealist as a person who knows that a rose is more beautiful than a cabbage and therefore believes that a rose will make better soup. I come here, as I said, as an idealist. I believe that the ideal is possible, if one works hard enough for it, but I have made soup. I know that cabbage makes better soup, so it is the ideal that I will strive to achieve here as a member of Parliament, ever mindful of the fact that it is soup which we need in Canada, cabbage soup. Ordinary folks' soup is what we need.

speechtext:
This is very obvious in the Speech from the Throne. It is a first things first speech. In it is demonstrated that long-term planning rather than short-term political expediency exists in government now.

October 16, 1979
The Address-Mrs. Stratas
As I said earlier, 1 am a novice member of this House, so I consider it fitting that I come here during the International Year of the Child. I am a child in some respects compared with some of the more senior and very respected members of the House, but 1 am not afraid to admit that I have much to learn, and I believe that sometimes innocence is an advantage. This is a new government; our slate is clean.
It is a particular honour, too, to take my seat in the House of Commons in the month of the fiftieth anniversary of the "persons" case. As I look around the House, it occurs to me to point out that at the present rate of increase the House will be half filled with women in 842 years! It is like a marriage; the first 100 years are the hardest. One consideration of a novice member in this House is the fear of losing credibility through, 1 am told, ill-advised or ill-considered espousement of a cause.
When the novice is like me, a woman, and the cause is women's rights, the fear is more than justifiable. No parliamentarian can afford to be branded, not if he expects to make any serious contribution to government. To speak too forcibly too soon for women's rights would be to brand myself as a feminist, which is pretty low, so to speak, generally on the credibility scale.
However, 50 years after the BNA Act came into effect women were not constitutionally recognized as persons. Women were not "persons in matters of rights and privileges but only persons in matters of pains and penalties". Moreover, the Supreme Court of Canada ruled that it would be dangerous to assume that women could be considered persons in terms of the BNA Act wording that the government summon "qualified persons" to the Senate. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council of Britain, at that time Canada's final court of appeal, overruled the Supreme Court decision, and I would like to quote exactly the words of the Privy Council decision.
The exclusion of women from all public office is a relic of days more barbarous than ours, and to those who ask why the word "person" should include females, the obvious answer is, "Why not?"
Fifty years ago I would not have been considered a person. Today I am a member of this very worthy House. Nevertheless, the fact remains that women form only 2.8 per cent of the complement of this House, although they form more than 50 per cent of the population of Canada. The fact remains, according to the national council on welfare report tabled just last week, that 16 per cent of adult Canadian women live in poverty; that is, one out of every six women manages to survive somehow on incomes below the Statistics Canada poverty line. The fact remains that in Canada two out of every three elderly widows have incomes below the poverty line, and less than one widow in four can expect to receive any regular benefits from her deceased husband's employer. The fact remains that 68 per cent of single mothers under age 35 have incomes below the poverty line. "I do not mind refusing them potato chips and cookies," one spouseless mother said, "but it really bothers me when I have to say no when they ask for a banana".
A traditional comment about women members of Parliament is that they tend to concentrate only on "soft" issues like health, social welfare, culture and the family, but it is my

belief that these so-called soft issues are the very fabric of society.

speechtext:
If the fabric is rotten or of inferior quality, then all the seams in the world will not hold it together. The facts prove, moreover, that women have shown interest, expertise and leadership in widely diverse areas of legislation and jurisdiction in the House. Private members' bills introduced by women have dealt with such matters as amendments to the Criminal Code, modernization of the Copyright Act, the creation of a department of consumer affairs and the regulation of election expenses as well as bills affecting women and maternity benefits, abortion and equal pay.
Much remains to be done in terms of legislation concerning women's rights. It must be remembered too that legislation must be implemented to be effective. Ambiguous or unenfor-cible legislation makes a mockery of law. This must be avoided above all else. What must also be avoided is the impatient shelving of women-related legislation on the ground that more urgent and weighty measures must be dealt with. What is more urgent than the lives of 50 per cent of the population of Canada? I do not advocate hasty, radical action, nor do I want to see legislation which is rhetorically admirable but practically unenforcible.
Long-term ramifications and ricochet reactions must be considered. It is no good to deal with today and to let tomorrow take care of itself. History has shown that tomorrow is notoriously unable to look after itself, partly because of shortsighted legislation which may have served the day but encumbered the future.
The Canadian suffragette movement was quite free from violence, believe it or not, compared with the United States and Great Britain. Canada witnessed a very quiet and orderly struggle for female suffrage, with many colourful, intelligent women lending their talent and their wit to a potentially explosive cause.
As I look around this House, I am reminded of Nellie McClung's mock parliament in Winnipeg in 1924. As "Premier McClung" she denied men the vote by turning the anti-suffragist arguments around. She concluded with: "Men's place is on the farm!"
It is in our best interests as parliamentarians, as Canadians and as human beings, to lead the way with just, equitable legislation on women-related concerns. Let us not wait for model legislation from other countries. The research has been done, the rhetoric spoken and the groundwork completed. This House has the authority, the talent and the power to be a world leader in this field.
You know, Mr. Speaker, that the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) has assigned to me the duties of Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State. I am deeply honoured and

October 16, 1979
I very much look forward to working with the minister. 1 reiterate words which he once spoke:
We have a burgeoning potential for cultural expression. Yet Canadian culture today is a state subsidized activity on the margins of economic enterprise. Canadian culture tomorrow could be the growth industry of the decade. It goes to the root of our philosophy as a party that workable incentives are a more efficient and acceptable alternative than state compulsion.
I should like to quote as well the words of Mr. Raymond Moriyama, the architect and planner who designed the beautiful Scarborough civic centre of which we in Scarborough are so proud. Mr. Moriyama said:
A man needs dignity to remain human, but personal dignity cannot sustain a man unless there is social recognition of this need. Freedom is accepting responsibility for one's action and caring for others, caring about questions and caring about answers. Life is full of contradictions, some intolerable, some to be transcended. One must be passionately disinterested to find a balance, committed yet neutral. Everything is important and nothing is important. There is a God-like potential in every one of us, and every child born is a new opportunity for this potential to emerge.
I believe in Canada. I believe in the people of Canada. I believe in the potential of this country, its natural potential, its cultural potential, its people potential. I believe in the traditions of our past as exemplified by generations of Canadians from many backgrounds and origins. I believe in our courage as a nation, and I believe in the integrity of this House. It is a privilege for me to join my good colleagues as the member for Scarborough Centre in this Thirty-first Parliament of Canada.
