speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 take this opportunity to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. Being myself among the newly elected, as indicated by the hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. MacDonald), I want to assure you of my unreserved loyalty and complete dedication to the task which, as a member of parliament, was assigned to me by the electors of the constituency of Timmins-Chapleau. I should like to congratulate you for your appointment as Speaker of the House, with the heavy responsibilities you fulfil with such dignity and wisdom.

Mr. Speaker, the riding of Timmins-Chapleau was formed just prior to the last election and is now made up of parts of the former ridings of Timmins, Cochrane and Nickel Belt. It is a large riding, 450 kilometers by 320 kilometers. The eastern boundary is at the town of Iroquois Falls, a very progressive pulp and paper producing community, which can and will only survive if the present government continues the strategies developed by the former to encourage and ensure reforestation access to resources and incentives for modernization.
To the west of Iroquois Falls is Timmins, the regional centre of the riding and one of the important cities in northern Ontario. A federal presence must be maintained and expanded in that city, through Air Canada, through improved and additional federal services, and with the help of federal corporations such as CDC, FBDB and DREE.
Continuing west on a lonely stretch of highway one encounters a village called Foleyet which owes its existence to the CNR and to the woods industry. Care must be taken to maintain basic services in such small settlements as Foleyet and Gogama. Because of the curtailment of daily passenger train services, they face a very serious reduction in postal services.
Sixty miles further, on route 101, is Chapleau, a lumber town on the CPR mainline. Here reside the typical northeners who, against almost insurmountable odds, have carved a permanent if difficult existence, never giving up, always striving for improvement while maintaining the perpetual optimism so typical of northern people.
Near beautiful Wawa which lies in close proximity to Lake Superior is a small hamlet named Hawk Junction which, through the lack of sensitivity of the present government, has lost the opportunity through a Canada Works program to move and erect a building which would have served as a recreation centre and fire hall.

October 16, 1979
The Address-Mr. Chenier
Finally, one arrives in Wawa, a mining and tourist centre where hospitality and friendliness permeate the atmosphere. This small town is nestled in the pre-Cambrian shield. At times it has had more difficulty to identify with the rest of Canada than some of the communities of the Territories. The former government established national communication links with Wawa. It now remains our task to permit it to identify with its region through special arrangements between the CBC and local television stations.
[ Translation]
When you go from Timmins to Sudbury you can visit all kinds of small communities such as Gogama, Cartier, Bis-cotasing, Kormac and Westree. Those people are independent. They do not ask much of the federal government. However, it would seem that on behalf of budgetary restrictions, those Canadians, those humble and simple people, will become the forgotten people of our nation.
[ English)
The riding of Timmins-Chapleau has five reservations. The Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) has indicated that measures would be presented to the House for the improvement of the plight of our native population. I welcome this promise and 1 hope that, as other promises, it will not disintegrate in confusion and retraction.
[ Translation]
Northern Ontario is my country. 1 live there and I have devoted most of my career to it. I know its people: they are optimistic, energetic, independent and proud. Whether of Canadian, European or Asiatic descent, we live there in harmony and unity. The northern Ontario inhabitants of the Timmins-Chapleau riding are a model for all the people of Canada of the flourishing of unity within diversity, of a unity based on respect and mutal acceptance.
I suggest that the parliamentary committee on multicultur-alism which will be set up soon should come and visit us in order to observe the results of such an attitude. Maybe we can pass on our spirit of unity to the rest of Canada.
This government is less than six months old and the citizens of Timmins-Chapleau have strong misgivings and mistrust in their first evaluation of the new administration, and for very specific reasons. The government had been in power less than two months when it decided to cut off our communities from job-creation funds which had previously been available through the Canada Works program.
This brings to mind a couple of issues the Tories advocated during the federal election and repeated in the Speech from the Throne. On the one hand the Speech from the Throne indicated that the government will introduce "measures to strengthen the role of the voluntary sector in our society", while on the other hand it arbitrarily cut off voluntary groups in all of Ontario from their noble task of creating, sponsoring

and selecting community-spirited job-creation projects by shelving Canada Works in many parts of Canada.
Canada Works was an important tool to deal with seasonal unemployment especially in areas with little economic stability. It is my hope that the new government will understand that many smaller communities will constantly live or die at the mercy of the economic indicators of more prosperous and larger communities. For example, it is not fair for the government to decide that such areas as Gogama, Cartier and Foleyet will not benefit from Canada Works, because Timmins, Iroquois Falls, Chapleau and Wawa industries are operating at full capacity in the mining, forestry and pulp and paper sectors. In everyday life Canada Works was the only tangible link the people of these smaller communities in Timmins-Chapleau riding had with the federal government. The program provided useful jobs while at the same time offering essential services which otherwise would not have been possible.
Permanent jobs were created in some areas. Now these communities have reverted to the style of the early sixties where these people will contribute to the federal coffers via taxes but will get little in return. It is my hope that the right hon. Prime Minister will rethink his perception, which is certainly not shared by myself. If the new government pursues this vision of Canada, of course, our country will be a community of communities, but communities strongly divided between large, prosperous one like Timmins, Wawa, Chapleau and Iroquois Falls, and small abandoned ones like Foleyet, Gogama and Cartier, communities which will have been left to fend for themselves by a central government that will have given away most of its power to keep the communities together. We have yet to see which better programs the Prime Minister intends to introduce in order to encourage young Canadians to serve their communities.
[ Translation]
Hardly three months after the new government came into power, my riding took another beating, since the new administration decided to scrap the decentralization program of the previous Liberal government and thus eliminate 109 jobs intended for Timmins. In my view, it makes good sense to break up the centralized machinery of government and make it more accessible to Canadians, and I believe this Liberal decision justified every dollar earmarked for this purpose.
The city of Timmins and the private sector in the region had been waiting since 1976 and there had been discussions regarding the integration of these jobs into the downtown renewal program. The people who had welcomed this move as a unique opportunity to diversify employment and as a means to ensure greater economic stability in a region which is closely related to the mining industry, cannot understand why the government has persisted in this decision. It seems to me that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) is obsessed with the idea of eliminating jobs and cutting expenditures inconsiderately and regardless of the impact on the municipali-

October 16, 1979
ties and those concerned. We can almost foresee the day when government spending will be so strictly controlled by the minister responsible for the Treasury Board that the Canadian people will laugh at the Progressive Conservatives' good intentions of placing greater reliance, to quote their very words, on individual initiative to generate growth and jobs for Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, 1 remind the new government that the decision to eliminate 109 jobs in Timmins was taken without consulting the parties concerned. Is that the kind of consultation and co-operation to be expected of the new government, as convincingly stated in the Speech from the Throne?

As if the Timmins-Chapleau riding has not suffered enough already since this government fumbled into office, judging from the Prime Minister's statements prior to his ascendancy to the highest office in the land 1 suspect that northern Ontario is in for further hardship at the hands of this government. I refer to the former opposition leader's remarks concerning air transportation in Canada and the role of Air Canada, our national airline and unifying national symbol.
As the former opposition leader may be aware, Timmins is a community of major importance in Canada with a population of almost 50,000. It is serviced by Air Canada, a service which is essential to the citizens in northern Ontario. Air Canada provides three flights a day both to and from Toronto, two of which make stopovers in North Bay. Although these stopovers are an inconvenience, we recognize Air Canada is at least trying to provide an adequate service to northern Ontario. All efforts to bring Timmins into closer contact with the larger centres in Canada will go to waste if the Prime Minister intends to keep another of his interminable, ill-advised pledges.
It was November, 1978 when the then opposition leader told the House the following:
Air Canada has been unwilling to give up its routes in southwestern and northern Ontario, where regional carriers should be operating.
In the same speech concerning his air transport policy the present Prime Minister, in a statement which may have set the precedent for such gems of conviction as "We will move our embassy to Jerusalem" and "We oppose raising interest rates," made the following declaration:
We will significantly increase the routes open to regional and third level carriers. It makes sense to have major trunk routes served by national carriers; it makes no sense to allow them to dominate regional and local services. Our general approach will be that regional routes of up to 300 miles and turnaround routes of up to 500 miles will be reserved for regional and third level carriers.
Unless the government remains consistent in its fickleness to promises made in the heat of battle and ignores but another policy brainchild, Timmins will be the victim again of this government and will lose its Air Canada service. I caution the government that the people of my riding will not stand still while the government robs it of an essential link with the rest of the nation. I will seek a guarantee that Air Canada service to Timmins will not be sacrificed as a part of this government's apparent commitment to privatize, abandon, sell or dismember the institutions of government which provide a sense of nation-
The Address-Mr. Chenier
al homogeneity and common purpose. I warn the government to tread lightly if it has any intention of slipping Air Canada service away from the citizens of northern Ontario. I take some small encouragement from the fact the government chose to refrain from mentioning air policy in the Speech from the Throne. Perhaps it did this after having given further consideration to some suggestions made prior to the election. [Translation]
Along with several crucial and vital questions, another matter of concern to the constituency of Timmins-Chapleau, in northern Ontario, as well as to several other parts of Canada, was left out of the Speech from the Throne. I refer to the forest industry which is one of the most important sectors of the Canadian economy and the livelihood of thousands of people in the northern part of the province. I represent a region where the pulp, paper and lumber industries are the economic basis of several communities. Those industries are extremely sensitive to export markets, production costs as well as to supply and demand. For instance, the people of Chapleau depend on six lumbermills for their livelihood. Thanks to the initiative of gifted entrepreneurs from northern Ontario, Chapleau has become a major supplier of wood products in both Canada and the United States. I do hope the future of the forest industry in my area and other regions as well will not be jeopardized by the measures the new government intends to take.
But I am alarmed at the prospects for the lumber industry in my riding and all of Canada if the government persists in the policies it contemplates. I refer to the hiking of interest rates and the mortgage deductibility scheme. 1 am told by an official of the Canadian Construction Association that for every percentage point the interest rate on capital is raised, the demand for housing drops by 10,000 units. If we are to believe that the mortgage deductibility goody will increase demand for capital, it will raise mortgage interest rates to even more intolerable levels. Does the government realize what impact these policies will have on the construction and lumber producing industries?
In addition to the soaring interest rates on capital, there are other serious problems facing the construction and lumber industries that this government must address itself to. The cost of lumber has risen 95 per cent since 1975. In the last two years alone, lumber has leaped 40 per cent in price. This has been due to the heavy demand for Canadian forest products in the United States and an almost 50 per cent increase in production costs. The danger in the present situation is obvious. Should the cost of capital and materials continue to rise at the rate they have been, the demand for housing will drop, regardless of the mortgage deductibility gimmick, and in so doing put lumber producers in peril.
I urge this government to consider the real consequences of its actions for the home buyer, the construction industry and
262

October 16, 1979
The Address-Mr. Cooper
the lumber producers if the cost of acquiring housing is driven out of the reach of the average citizen. I urge the government to ponder its actions carefully before another election promise made in desperation backfires and renders severe damage to these sensitive industries of northern Ontario.

Because of the policies implemented by the former government, the mining industry is healthy today. Our mines are flourishing and going ahead with major expansion projects. Texas Gulf, which mines zinc, copper and silver, is buoyant and is in the process of completing a refinery. The iron ore mine of Algoma Steel, located at Wawa, is operating at full capacity. For over a year now, the mining industry inspires confidence in the future. If we want that climate of full employment to extend throughout the mining industry, it is essential for the federal government to introduce measures that will sustain the current impetus and ensure even more investments in all fields of operation and development. [English]
The riding of Timmins-Chapleau is very large indeed. It is a microcosm of Canada. It strives on diversity-diversity of language, diversity of culture, of race, of belief. Each small region lives on a particular industry different from the others. Each town, each village, each hamlet, prides itself on its achievements, its hopes, its participation in the Canadian mosaic.
We also believe that there must be a federal presence among ourselves, a presence that symbolizes that our diversity is not adverse to unity, that all parts of Canada make up the Canadian people, that none must suffer to remain Canadian if all are willing to give a little. Canada will not survive if all the parts demand special status or special privileges. I plead with the Prime Minister and the cabinet to ponder their present approach to bonne entente. Do not let political expediency take precedence over the need to keep Canada as one strong nation.

Mr. Speaker, my first duty upon rising is to convey my very sincere congratulations to the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker upon their appointment, and to you, sir, as Deputy Chairman of Committees, upon your appointment. I can say as one who is new to this House but who has had the opportunity over the years to view the proceedings of this House of Parliament on television that the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker, and you, sir, have the loyalty and the support of each and every member of this House, and that that loyalty and support is very well deserved indeed.
My second very pleasant duty is to convey my heartiest congratulations to the other two members of Parliament who spoke first as the mover and seconder of this motion, the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) and the hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. MacDonald). I can say, speaking again as a new member, that they set for me, and for all of us as new members here in Parliament, a very high standard indeed, one which I hope one day we will be able to attain.

I am very glad to have been elected as the member of Parliament for Halifax. Indeed, I might even say that I am relieved to have been elected as member of Parliament for Halifax. I think that I have the distinction of being the member in this House with the smallest majority in all of Canada, 15 votes.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You have 14 more than you need.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My distinguished predecessor, the Hon. Robert L. Stanfield, said something very similar. He said to me, "Fifteen votes, don't you think that is overkill? You only need one, you know." I will be talking in a minute about the hon. Mr. Stanfield. My present point is that whether it be one vote, 15 votes or 15,000 votes, it will be my privilege, duty and honour to serve all of the people of the constituency of Halifax, whatever party they support, to the best of my ability, and I look forward to that task very much.
Tradition requires a new member of parliament making his maiden speech to say a few words about his constituency, and I am happy indeed to do so in the case of Halifax because in all this world there can be few communities, I suggest, which are so civilized and yet so close to wild and beautiful nature, so respectful of tradition and yet so eager to look ahead, so lively in the clash of ideas and yet where people are so tolerant of one another.
I could talk about the physical aspects of Halifax, the fact that we have the world's best natural harbour, standing astride the world's busiest shipping lanes, sitting virtually on top of the world's richest fishing grounds. I could talk at length about the historical facts, how Halifax was founded in 1749 and came to be the bastion of British imperial power, military and naval, in North America, how it carried on in that way for a century and a half, and as Canada's major naval station carries on that role today. I could talk about that symbol of Canada which is known the world over, the Halifax Citadel and the old town clock which, incidentally, constitutes the most visited historical site in all of Canada. In that same vein I could talk about how Halifax's social history has been inexorably linked with peace keeping and war making.
I could tell how in 1917 the largest man-made explosion in the history of the world until Hiroshima occurred as a result of a collision in Halifax harbour of a munitions ship and a supply ship during the First World War and killed 2,000 people from the city of Halifax, almost as if they had been at the front lines. I could talk about the convoys of allied merchantmen and fighting ships of World War II, most of which used Halifax as their base from which to build a bridge from the new world to the old. Rather than take refuge in the dull facts of geography and dry dust of history, however, I want to talk about the people of Halifax, and particularly about the most famous adopted son in the history of Halifax, the Hon. Robert L. Stanfield.
Robert Stanfield, a man known to all in his former constituency of Halifax and to everyone in this House as well as to all
October 16, 1979

Canadians, is an example of the very best we can offer in political life. He is a great man, a humble man, a strong man, a magnanimous man, a proud man, a compassionate man, a man who has done more than any living Canadian to bring us together as a people and to heal the wounds of division in this great country.
If, in due time, I were able to become the kind of representative in Parliament that my predecessor, Bob Stanfield, was, I would then regard myself as a fitting representative of the people of Halifax. I promise to them to work toward that goal and I thank them profoundly for placing their confidence in me.
Parliament is an institution that Bob Stanfield loved. So did another great Canadian and another leader of the Progressive Conservative Party, the late Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker.
I was personally delighted to hear in the Speech from the Throne, which is the subject of this debate, that the new Progressive Conservative Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Clark) plans to restore to Parliament its true role in our democratic system by making the government and the bureaucracy more accountable to Parliament than before. There can be no doubt that in the last decade or two Parliament has been gravely weakened in relation to its powers to control government and bureaucracy. The result has been a corresponding strengthening of those two elements in our lives. If we, as Canadians, are going to keep the power we now have to control government and the bureaucracy, and if we are going to wrest away some of the power that has been taken from us in the past few years, then I suggest that all members of this House must pursue the government's stated goal with vigour and with determination. I see that vigour and determination on all sides in this House, Mr. Speaker, and I see it in every party. If I may say so, I see it especially in many of the new members who have come to this House. All of them are here, I believe, Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Cardigan said in his speech seconding this motion, to try to make Parliament work.
In this respect, Mr. Speaker, I was frankly very disappointed in the opening remarks of the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Lalonde) in this debate, in which he said he found it humorous that the Rhinoceros party, the joke party from the province of Quebec, had done so well in his constituency in the last federal election, as it did across that province. 1 do not find that situation humorous at all, Mr. Speaker. To me, it is rather a sign of just how far Parliament has fallen into contempt in the eyes of many Canadians as a result of eleven years of government guided by the hon. member and his friends. I say with great sincerity to the hon. member that he should change his attitude, and join with those of us who have come to Parliament to try to make it work in following the suggestion of the Prime Minister that Parliament be given new life in this thirty-first assembly.
There were a number of aspects of the throne speech that will be particularly appealing to the people of Halifax. The first was the promise by the new government to re-establish the spirit of partnership in confederation-to replace a policy
The Address-Mr. Cooper
of confrontation with one of co-operation. We sorely need a change in the climate of federal-provincial relations. The new government got off to a good start, as far as we in Nova Scotia are concerned, when it offshore announced that Nova Scotia would have jurisdiction over its offshore mineral resources from now on.
Some hon. members on the other side have asked why this is so important to us in Nova Scotia. They point to the understanding reached by the former government and the maritime provinces whereby 75 per cent of the benefits of the offshore resources would accrue to the coastal provinces, and the federal government would take 25 per cent. They point out, and I think quite fairly, that the cost of administering that offshore resource, which would have been borne by the federal government under the previous proposal, would probably eat up the whole of that 25 per cent.
1 certainly agree that the net economic benefits in terms of royalties to the coastal provinces under the new arrangement, which has not yet been worked out in detail but which has been promised in principle, may not be all that different from the previous agreement.
In my view there are two very good reasons for dropping the proposal of the former government and adopting the proposal of the new government in relation to offshore resources. First of all, Nova Scotia has a vital interest in being able to control and direct the economic development that will inevitably come to the province as oil and gas are discovered offshore, in a way that best suits the needs of the people who live there. These needs can be assessed and acted upon by the people on the spot, the provincial government of the province of Nova Scotia, and not by bureaucrats, or even politicians from the province, who happen to be here in Ottawa.
The second and more important reason is that jurisdiction over the offshore resources gives to the province of Nova Scotia a new hinterland to exploit and develop. In my view it will help us to acquire a sense of pride and confidence in ourselves that is so essential if we are to realize the economic and the community spiritual values that we ought to be able to attain, as this resource is developed.
The second major thrust of the throne speech that will be particularly well received by my constituents, the citizens of Halifax, reads as follows:
The greatest immediate challenge facing Canada today is to restore growth, confidence, and jobs to the Canadian economy.
In setting out its five-part strategy on this matter the government emphasized its proposal to build on the strengths of the various regions in the country. It talked in particular, in relation to the constituents of Halifax, about shipbuilding and about a Canadian merchant marine. I can say without any hesitation that there could not be two proposals better construed to help put the unemployed back to work in Halifax and to create a sound economic future than those two. I would like to explain to the House that only two years ago as many as 1,600 men and women were employed in the Halifax shipyard. As a result of a slowdown in work and a change in ownership

October 16, 1979
The Address-Mr. Cooper
of the company in question, the number dropped to 300 at the lowest point.
The Prime Minister has obviously recognized, in the 200-year tradition of shipbuilding and the pride of craftsmanship that exists in the city of Halifax and the Atlantic provinces, that there is a regional strength upon which to build those particular industries and upon which to build the Atlantic region of Canada. For that reason I commend the government for recognizing this strength and for its proposal to build on it.
My constituents will also be happy to see the government's proposal to strengthen the mandate of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. When the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Trudeau) became Prime Minister in 1968 he raised great hopes in Atlantic Canada that at last we would be able to begin the long climb toward economic equality with the rest of Canada as his concept of the just society took effect. And, to his credit, he did set up DREE giving it the job of working with provincial governments toward that equality.
What is the state of affairs in Atlantic Canada today, ten years after DREE was established? Unfortunately, DREE has not worked entirely successfully, Mr. Speaker. Yes, it has pumped hundreds of millions of dollars into the economy of Atlantic Canada. Yes, it has provided much needed infrastructure for our towns, cities, industries and commercial ventures there. Yes, DREE has provided many millions of dollars to commercial enterprises to help them get under way. But since 1969 the average income for Canadians living in Atlantic Canada has risen from 70.2 per cent to only 74.1 per cent of the Canadian average. At this rate it would take us a full 60 years to catch up. And, what is worse, if you take from those figures the portion attributable to transfer payments to individuals, such as unemployment insurance, the percentages show that we have gained hardly at all compared to the Canadian average. The figures have risen from 65.6 per cent to only 66.8 per cent in one decade. In short, our net gains in Atlantic Canada have come from feeding out of the government trough. By far, we would rather have work than have to live on unemployment insurance. As it is, we are in grave danger of becoming a dependent society incapable of acting on our own, and able to carry on only because of a permanent "fix" of federal funds.
This state of affairs must end. It must end not only because of the financial drain on Canadians who live elsewhere in Canada who are required to sluice their money in great quantities, in ever increasing amounts, to Atlantic Canada. But also it must end because of the spiritual and social malaise that this kind of dependency brings about in those who receive this kind of money as gifts.
1 believe that we in Atlantic Canada, a once proud people and a still proud people, are in danger of losing belief in ourselves, belief in our own ability to get on with the job, without which we will not only stagnate but stagnate unhappily. I do not believe that anyone who is in a permanently dependent state is happy.

How do we in Parliament move to end this state of affairs, Mr. Speaker? As I said, the previous government, in good conscience, tried to solve the problem of regional disparity by creating DREE to deal with it. But it was in those times a weak sister. There were always other, bigger, departments of government whose concerns overrode DREE. They often wiped out at a stroke, often times unintentionally, or unthink-lingly, all the good that DREE had done. What is the use of spending millions of dollars on manufacturing plants in Atlantic Canada if a national policy of user-pay is adopted by the Department of Transport in such a way that it is no longer possible for our manufacturing plants to ship goods or sell them competitively in the markets of central Canada? What is the use of spending millions of dollars for infrastructure to assist commercial and industrial development in Atlantic Canada if the Foreign Investment Review Agency is set up to screen out foreign investment, not only in central Canada where such screening may make sense but also in Atlantic Canada where there is hardly any industry to begin with?
it is not enough to continue to dole out more and more money to the needy provinces, cities, towns, companies and individuals who live there, and hope to solve our problems in that way. To be sure we need to have this money in the short term just to stay alive. But in the longer term we must instead put regional concerns at the very centre of policy-making in this country. We must examine each policy and each program of each department of government, not only DREE, and we must apply to those policies and programs this test: how will this policy or that program affect the economy of every region of this country? Then we must tailor-make those policies and programs to fit the particular needs of each region of Canada.
I believe our new Prime Minister understands this point very well. He has lived in every region of Canada. He was born and raised on the prairies. He lived for a year in my own constituency of Halifax. He has lived on the west coast of Canada, and of course he has lived in the central region of the country. He has seen at first-hand the diversity of this country and the differing needs of each and every part. The Prime Minister understands that we here in Parliament in Ottawa can only attain Canadian unity and economic strength by respecting those differences and by building on the strengths of each of the regions.
When the Speech from the Throne refers to strengthening the mandate of DREE, and about taking into account regional needs, I hope and believe that the Prime Minister and the government have in mind a mechanism for ensuring that these regional concerns will be reflected in the policies and programs of all departments from now on.
In 1878 Sir John A. Macdonald, Prime Minister of Canada, proclaimed his famous "national policy." This policy was founded on three programs: a coast to coast railway; large scale immigration from the old world to Canada; and a tariff barrier to protect and develop central Canadian industry. This was a good policy for Canada. Indeed, it was an essential policy. Without it we would never have become a large scale manufacturer of secondary products, of manufactured goods
October 16, 1979

nor would we have been able to build the rich and modern land that we have today. Yet this national policy was unashamedly directed at building up the central region of this country to the exclusion-one might almost say at the expense-of another, the Atlantic region.
In 1878 Atlantic Canada had a highly developed commercial sector. Atlantic Canada carried on a sophisticated trade with our natural north-south trading partner, the United States of America. While there were many goods we did not make ourselves, we could import those goods cheaply from the United States and other countries without any tariff or customs duties. Sir John A. Macdonald's national policy changed all that. The new tariff barriers cut off cheap imports from the United States. And the retaliatory tariff barriers raised against us made it difficult for Atlantic Canada to sell goods abroad. Nevertheless, I do not complain about Sir John A. Macdonald's national policy. I praise it. It was a necessary policy in the interest of developing the great Canadian hinterland, even if it did hurt Atlantic Canada.
The time has come to try to redress that balance once and for all. Let all of us in this Thirty-first Parliament set ourselves a goal. Let us adopt a new national policy, unashamedly directed at building up those regions of Canada which remain economically deprived 101 years after Sir John A. Macdonald's national policy. Let us not think of these programs as being regional ones. Rather, let us think of them as being national ones, designed to build on the strength of the deprived regions for the benefit of all Canada. Let us know and believe the truth, that it is only when we have strong and healthy economic regions in Canada that we can have a strong and healthy nation.
In closing, I wish to thank the people of Halifax for sending me here as their representative. I look forward to working closely with members on all sides of the House as together we serve the country we love, Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as everyone knows, 75 per cent of Quebeckers polled recently on behalf of the Quebec government said they would insist on a renewed constitution as the only condition to remain within Canada. Is the Progressive Conservative government going to negotiate sovereignty-association as it did for natural resources? Will its
The Address-Mrs. Hervieux-Payette preoccupation to please the provinces go that far? On May 22, Quebeckers did not trust the Progressive Conservative Party and maybe they were right, because they do not feel this party understands them. It offers no clear action on the constitutional issue, no guarantee for the survival of French Canadians, as there was in Bill C-60. No mention of the human rights bill, no mention of patriation of the constitution or of amendment formula, no linguistic and cultural guarantee. In short, Quebec is still waiting and will probably wait forever for the Progressive Conservative government to take a precise stand on the constitutional question.
Just last night, Mr. Speaker, Mr. Rene Levesque, speaking in Hull, promised to absorb federal public servants no more than two years after winning the referendum. How does the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Jarvis) intend to counter such assertions? Is he going to negotiate the transfer to Quebec of federal public servants? Perhaps this would enable him to implement the promises made during the electoral campaign about cutting manpower. Does the Clark government show a sense of responsibility when it abdicates in favour of the provinces without demanding anything to maintain some kind of equilibrium at the central level? Indeed it abdicates its responsibilities in the field of economics by leaving to the private sector the task of planning the future of Canadians. It abdicates its responsibilities toward all the minorities, be it on a cultural or social level. The only voice from the minorities that it seems to pay attention to is that of the multinationals. They may represent a numerical minority but they certainly do not when it comes to power. When will the Clark government start governing in the interest of all Canadians? When will it be through paying off its electoral debts?
After hearing the proposals contained in the Speech from the Throne, Mr. Speaker, with regard to the housing issue, I am left asking myself some serious questions such as to whom is this policy directed? Is it designed for the majority which dwells in expensive houses and whose taxes take a large share of the budget already higher than those who will also have to foot the bill? Where do we find measures which will help workers buy their houses? Where do we find a housing credit for single mothers or the elderly? Where do we find a sense of equity in the housing policy of the Progressive Conservative government?
In the Speech from the Throne, Mr. Speaker, there is also a commitment to reduce government expenses. Who is going to pay for those reductions? People who get old age pension, family allowances or unemployment benefits? Once again, Mr. Speaker, I wonder who the Progressive Conservative government is governing for.
We could only be pleased with that promise to reduce expenses in the public service, since the former government itself had come forward with major budget cuts last year. However, we notice that during the six months since this

October 16, 1979
The Address-Mrs. Hervieux-Payette government was elected, so many people have been hired to work in the office of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) that a new bureaucracy is obviously growing within his cabinet. Some public servants who are not very high in that hierarchy and who are in a position to speak without fear, even told us that there have been more favouritism and political appointments in the last six months than in the last ten years before this government took power. How many more political appointments are they still planning to make, Mr. Speaker? While there is an indication in the Speech from the Throne that there will be a reduction in the number of public servants, 1 do not know of any mention about an increase in the number of friends of the party in power within government.
May I remind them that the last CROP poll, which was published yesterday, still gives them the support of only 37 per cent of the voters, compared with 41 per cent to the Liberals, and that it would be dangerous to govern only for those 37 per cent. I urge them to have faith in the public service, which has no partisanship and which always considered that it was its duty to serve all Canadians. What does the Progressive Conservative Party want to do with Canada? A society with more justice, or a society which will follow the dictates of Gallup polls?
For young workers, Mr. Speaker, this Speech from the Throne contains a very important measure, namely, the promise of jobs. How does the government intend to carry out that promise? By opening new offices, thus creating jobs for those who will be working in those new offices? There are now, Mr. Speaker, hiring centres like Canada Manpower Centres on campuses and I think there are quite enough of them. 1 would rather urge the Progressive Conservative government to go and see their business friends to ask them to hire those young people.
For large and low income families, for older people, who is going to pay the bill for their food basket which is going to increase substantially, at least 10 per cent, if the oil pricing policy of this government is implemented? For them, one only has to know that it represents up to 27 per cent of their income and one wonders whether that amount and percentage can be further increased without any thought of rebellion on their part. Personally we are going to fight relentlessly such inequity because the social impact of such a move is such that it can lead to a general downgrading of the quality of life for the Canadian people, in addition to affecting seriously the health of the aged.
Mr. Speaker, with respect to the freedom of information act, we can only be pleased with it. And we hope it will be fully implemented on the basis of objective criteria that will give all groups, as well as parliamentarians, access to government information. However, that kind of legislation should not be a cover-up for such intentions as revealing to officials the conclusions of a report even before it is written. The Middle East issue is an example.


With the perspective of encouraging individual initiative and promoting private enterprise, because these are the principles of modern liberalism, I intend to propose a bill to promote profit sharing. Within the state of actual fiscal policy there does not exist any mechanism to instil in private enterprise the wish to return to the employees their share in the profits made in the fiscal year, other than pension plans, and these too are limited.
1 propose using the tax structure to provide an incentive to companies to return a portion of their profits to their employees, by reducing their actual rate of taxation for that portion. On the other hand, for the employees who receive these benefits the tax structure would be amended in such a way as to reduce the rate of tax on their portion of the profits, adding to their net income. The goal of this measure would be to initiate a positive dialogue between the company and its employees in order to reach the common objective, which is the financial success of the enterprise.
This measure would help to demystify the question of profits and remove from it the immoral character it has received at the hands of socialist ideology. Moreover, this profit sharing scheme would enhance co-operation between employer and employee, which in turn should lead to an increase in production. An additional asset of this plan would be to reduce the number of strikes by making employers and employees partners instead of opponents.
The Progressive Conservative government promises in the Speech from the Throne to look after working women, with an employment strategy, and I can only welcome that. However, what do they intend to do for women who stay at home and who are now at the bottom of the social ladder? According to a recent report released by the National Council on Social Welfare last October, 1,219,000 women in Canada, one out of six, lived below the poverty line. In that category are included 44 per cent of women who are heads of families with dependent children. That latter category includes 50 per cent who do not receive alimony or who must get it by fighting in court.
Mr. Speaker, I intend to introduce a bill on the compulsory collection of alimony on behalf of those women, since they are not represented in this House. We shall not accept the jurisdictional argument which was used for too long as an excuse for inaction. Canadian women with dependent children should be given priority by the Canadian government in this period of low birth-rate. Why punish a woman who wants to stay home to raise her children by forcing her to live on welfare? The federal government has a responsibility in this matter since it contributes 50 per cent of the provincial welfare funds. It has therefore a direct interest in this matter. These funds could be used to improve the lot of the community as a whole and of the needy, and could be reduced in the years to come.
October 16, 1979

If the Clark government would only see in this a means of relieving the taxpayers' burden, they might understand that they could achieve a dual objective by taking such a measure. On the one hand, they would reduce the amounts appropriated for social programs and increase the national productivity as all those in receipt of alimony payments guaranteed and collected by the state in case of default by the husband would not be automatically deprived of part-time work. Of course, this measure would also apply when the father must stay home to take care of his family.
This is why I ask that the Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs meet urgently to discuss this matter and prepare immediately a proposal for the next federal-provincial conference for the approval of the provinces in principle. The spirit of co-operation which prevails in this government should ensure the passage of such a measure in the interests of all Canadian men and women.
Mr. Speaker, with your permission, I should now like to deal with my special concerns for the Montreal area. The economic propects are rather gloomy at present. The strike in the port of Montreal may well have an indirect impact on food costs in the forthcoming season. The province of Quebec, with an adverse balance in agriculture, cannot afford to see food costs rise unduly. We hope that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Alexander) will take the necessary steps to solve this conflict before freeze-up.
Furthermore, the work at Place Guy Favreau is progressing very slowly. We ask the minister responsible to speed up the work, particularly in view of the problems facing construction workers every winter.
As concerns the chronic problem of public transportation, after the 8-month strike in Quebec City, the current Montreal strike is causing serious prejudice to the economy of the province. So we call for a study on public transportation in large centres in consultation with the provincial governments, because we keep in mind that the users of public transportation cannot express their views, particularly older people and students.
At this stage, Mr. Speaker, I wish to express my deepest gratitude to my constituents for the confidence they put in me on May 22 last. I consider it as a very great responsibility and I shall strive in the coming months to serve the interests of all. As you may know already, Mr. Speaker, my riding is located at the far end of the island of Montreal. It is largely made up of workers who are now suffering from an unacceptable unemployment situation for an urban area, at a rate of 9.5 per cent. However, since for the Progressive Conservative government there is a national average and another standard for job-creation programs, I must say that we are very concerned with the coming of winter. The Canada Works program has been reduced by half, but no alternative has been proposed to deal with the problems that will crop up this winter. So we are most eager to see the economic development strategy that the Clark
The Address-Mrs. Hervieux-Payette government intends to adopt in metropolitan Montreal. Let me say that we already have an interesting industrial infrastructure. What is lacking above all is the confidence of investors.
What steps does the Clark government intend to take to ensure eventual investors in Quebec that they have no particular problems to fear in Quebec in the present state of things?
Is the Progressive Conservative majority, which was elected mainly out of Quebec, willing to give the guarantees necessary to ensure the fulfillment of Quebeckers in Canada? After more than ten years of reflection, has the Progressive Conservative government found the magical words which will bring all Canadians together without abdicating its responsibilities? This afternoon the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) said that the former government was the cause of all our problems. Allow me to have a different opinion than my distinguished colleague and let me say that the former government certainly made every effort to bring Canadians together in a new direction towards a new Canada. The citizens of Mercier who have elected a PQ representative for nine years now expect more than a vague promise when it comes to future commitments.
Instead of dealing hastily with the energy problem, the Progressive Conservative government should plan the development of all national resources, without penalizing provinces that are poorer in raw materials, by diversifying renewable and non-renewable resources. In Eastern Quebec in particular, we are counting on the forthcoming development of the natural gas system, as well as on measures to promote increased development of that resource that is being underutilized in eastern Canada. We therefore recommend early studies to develop the gas potential in Baffin Island in order to shorten the Eastern provinces' supply lines.
In the energy area, and development in particular, I would point out that the former Liberal government did not hinder development in the western provinces, but rather promoted it. We expect the western premier will do the same for the eastern energy potential. On the issue of community housing for the underprivileged and the aged, we invite the government, in view of the throne speech, to plan its intended actions in that area carefully. The constituency of Mercier does not have a population of executives living in houses worth $100,000 and up, but rather a population of workers and pensioners who need housing at reasonable cost.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me invite my colleagues opposite, and especially the cabinet ministers, to visit the province of Quebec and get acquainted with the problem there. As a member of Parliament elected to maintain Quebec in Confederation, I urge hon. members to realize the urgency and seriousness of the situation. I speak on behalf of Francophones, Anglophones and newcomers who also are expecting concrete actions from a government that has almost no representation from Quebec.

The Address-Mr. Siddon

We are waiting for a sign in English-speaking Canada, for friendship, for the rebuilding of a new country in which equal rights are recognized for both groups. If I am here today, Mr. Speaker, it is to make sure that this dream cherished by most Quebeckers will come true.

Mr. Speaker, may I add my felicitations to those of other members who have congratulated you upon your re-election to the chair. I am pleased to speak in support of the motion, to thank His Excellency the Governor General for his most gracious Speech from the Throne.
I would also like to compliment the hon. member who has just preceded me. She spoke from her heart about her concern for all of Canada, and I am sure we will all give heed to her plea to those of us who perhaps do not understand French Canada as well as we should, to find ways of enabling this country to work together more effectively in the future.
I wish also to compliment my hon. friend from Erie (Mr. Fretz) and my hon. friend from Cardigan (Mr. MacDonald) for the fitting way in which they moved and seconded the motion of thanks to His Excellency.
This day, October 16, is a very special day for me, as it happens to be the anniversary of my first election to Parliament in a by-election one year ago. I feel fortunate to have had the privilege of sitting in opposition for a few months because it gave me a useful exposure to the serious defects of the former government which led to its downfall on May 22. I think we have all learned some lessons from that. If our many new initiatives, as so clearly set out in the throne speech, are allowed to bear fruit, I expect to be viewing my old seat from this more enlightened position on Mr. Speaker's right for many years to come.
Today is also a very special day for me in other respects as well. First, it was a very great privilege for me to take my seat in this Thirty-first Parliament with a man who is one of the finest examples of public stewardship. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) was the commissioner of my wolf cub pack when I joined it in Drumheller, Alberta, over 30 years ago. By that time he had already been a provincial MLA for almost ten years.
Indeed, in 40 years of public service, much of it as a cabinet minister in the Alberta government, the hon. member for Bow River has proved himself to be an outstanding and dedicated servant to the people of Alberta.

speechtext:
It was this man who gave me my first and strongest perspectives of what it means truly to serve humankind by virtue of elected office, and I am sure all in this House will benefit from his wisdom and counsel.
I am also proud to share a place in this Parliament with the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams). He is a
[Mrs. Hervieux-Payette.)
October 16, 1979
great Canadian of firm political conviction. He possesses a deep respect for the true principles of justice.
I will always remember that day in 1957 when the hon. member for Calgary North came to my home town of Drumheller, riding in a brightly coloured convertible. At his side was Canada's future Prime Minister, the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert. That evening in the local arena Dief spoke, just as he always spoke, with great oratory and passion about his love of Canada and his concern for those less prosperous parts and peoples of Canada whose needs had been neglected for decades by the dominant establishment in central Canada.
As a young man of 15 I was impressed by his message, and to this day I must credit John Diefenbaker with the kindling of my interest in our system of parliamentary democracy and in the political idealogies which shape it. I know he aroused those instincts in the hearts of many who sit in this Parliament today, especially some of my younger colleagues on this side of the House. It was a genuine honour to have known such a man and to have shared this place with him during those last few months of his life. He made Parliament live in a way which few others can. He made it accessible to every one of his 'fellow Canadians". I know that his inspiration will carry on in the lives of those who follow.
Indeed, it is one of those who followed who now leads the government of this great nation as our Prime Minister (Mr. Clark). The right hon. member for Yellowhead has come a long way from those days at the University of Alberta when I remember him as the controversial, outspoken young editor of our campus newspaper, The Gateway. In fact he has come a long way in the short time since May 22 of this year. By his example he has shown us how to be optimistic about the future potential of this great nation. At the same time he has developed strength of leadership to make his promise become a reality. His strength was never more plainly revealed to the members of this House than it was last Wednesday afternoon, when the Prime Minister delivered his first and very excellent speech to this Thirty-first Parliament. I believe that all Canadians will find his style of leadership to be a refreshing change from that of his immediate predecessor.
If hon. members would indulge me I would like to take a few moments now to tell them something about the part of Canada which I am privileged to represent. The riding of Richmond-South Delta is situated at the lower reaches of the Fraser River, encompassing most of the fertile soils and biologically productive marshes of the Fraser River delta. The northern-most community of Richmond is home for almost 100,000 Canadians who live on a beautiful island known as Lulu Island. The island has an elevation entirely at or below sea level, being completely surrounded by dikes and crisscrossed by countless drainage ditches. These drainage ditches provide flood protection not only from the Fraser River but also from the occasional winter rains which some may have heard about, and which are sent our way from the city of Vancouver, located to our immediate north.
October 16, 1979

Richmond is a progressive, well-planned, and growing city which offers a unique balance of natural habitat, agricultural production, beautiful gardens, parks, recreational facilities, light industries, and pleasant residential neighbourhoods. It is also the site of Vancouver International Airport, which occupies Sea Island, to the immediate northwest of the downtown centre of Richmond.
To the south of Richmond lies the municipality of Delta, located between the south arm of the Fraser River and the United States border. I am privileged to share in the representation of Delta with my good friend and colleague, the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen). My portion of Delta includes the two communities of Tsaw-wassen and Ladner. Tsawwassen is a modern and quite prosperous community known for its almost perpetual sunshine, pleasant beaches, and good community spirit. It shares a short international boundary with Point Roberts, U.S.A.-and votes rather conservatively, 1 might add.
To the north of Tsawwassen, on the south shore of the Fraser River, lies the historic farming and fishing community of Ladner. Ladner reminds me most of my own hometown because it is a small community with a deep sense of its history and an instinct for survival, as witnessed by the many small businesses which consolidate the town centre.
Delta and Richmond both grew out of the pioneering enterprise of the farmers and fishermen who came to settle on the soggy marshes of the Fraser River. In November of this year each municipality celebrates the hundredth anniversary of its incorporation, and many centennial events have been held throughout the year. In those days of 100 years ago a group of Japanese immigrants established a fishing village at the southwest corner of Lulu Island. Other settlers came from the British Isles and eastern Canada. Soon, fishing villages, wharves and canneries had sprung up all along the lower reaches of the Fraser River. As a result the communities of Steveston and Ladner remain today as an important focus for the commercial fishing industry of southern British Columbia. The Japanese who came to find their new life in Canada have flourished as a strong and respected source of cultural diversity in our midst.
On the nearby farmland, diked and drained with a century of toil, our people grow blueberries, strawberries, raspberries, cranberries, and vegetables of every description. Waterfront industries and urban development are also welcomed by my communities, and they have been allowed to proliferate because of their strategic importance to our economy and to our citizens. But the people of Richmond-South Delta are ever conscious of their links with the river, where wild fowl and young salmon flourish, nurtured by the natural habitat which rests in such fragile balance with the progress of mankind.
Of course, I shall have many future opportunities to tell this House of the problems and needs of my constituents, but for today I thought 1 would merely give a travelogue and a sense of the spirit of those 1 am privileged to represent here. I am grateful for the trust which they have placed in me once again, and I will do my utmost to serve them well.
The Address-Mr. Siddon
1 want to turn now to the throne speech directly and to underscore what I feel to be the central message from His Excellency. I believe that the throne speech provides us with a blueprint for a new spirit of co-operation and mutual trust within this great nation. By recognizing our regional, cultural and institutional differences as genuine assets, we can use them as tools to rediscover that positive spirit of optimism and innovation which possessed the Fathers of Confederation more than 100 years ago. As the Prime Minister has so frequently pointed out, we in Canada have many strengths on which to build, but the process must start here in Parliament which, after all, is little more than a microcosm of all the diverse attitudes and aspirations of Canadians. The throne speech states that, and I quote:
The great immediate challenge facing Canada today is to restore growth, confidence and jobs to the Canadian economy.
1 believe that goal can only be achieved if we can first of all purge our society of a serious illness which has infiltrated the attitude of Canadians in recent years. That illness I will call the illness of distrust. I believe that this illness is not visible in the deteriorating relationship which has developed in recent years between this federal government and the thousands of private sector businesses which form the backbone of our economy.
But this illness is not restricted to relations between government and private businesses. It is to be found also in the attitude of government bureaucracy toward the individual citizen, and in the distrust of the citizen toward his government. It is to be found in the relationship between provinces and the federal government, in the relationship between French and English Canada, between labour and management, between native peoples and non-natives, pro-nucs and anti-nucs, and of course between the opposition and government sides of this House.
I believe that this sickness must be cured, and it will be cured if we find a way to replace confrontation with compromise; if we can sacrifice self interest for the sake of the common good; if we can refrain from intentional exaggeration, and selective mis-use of statistics to argue a point.
On that score I should like to cite an example. We regularly hear in this House from some hon. members, particularly on the other side, of the so-called high rates of profiteering by certain industries in our country. I suggest that the rates that are cited are selectively chosen to discredit certain of the private sector corporations in this country. By selectively quoting percentage profit increases, without any honest attempt being made to tie these profit increases to the base profit for the previous year, Canadians are given a distorted and misleading impression that some corporations are making windfall profits. But a 50 per cent profit increase over a 4 per cent return on investment amounts to only a 6 per cent return on investment.
What these hon. members do not explain to the people of Canada is that if return on investment is lower than the

October 16, 1979
The Address-Mr. Siddon
interest rate on bonds or loans, then there will be no capital investment in speculative ventures, and with no money invested in this country far fewer jobs will be created, unless of course the federal government decides to step in, as it did for the past decade, and continually finance make-work projects, with increasing amounts of debt capital. As an aside, let me say that I would welcome from hon. members opposite in the coming days an explanation or a justification of ever increasing deficits. I would welcome it particularly from our good friends down in the far corner of the Elouse.
Another example of distrust which I feel is often displayed in the Elouse occurs whenever an hon. member makes sweeping insinuations about certain companies which may or may not be under investigation, or when a member casts doubt on the motives of another member. I saw this happen in recent days when an hon. member made reference to a certain meeting among three cabinet ministers, and tried to suggest a less than proper motive for that meeting. I believe that this sort of star chamber justice, this attempt to find ghosts where none exist, has no place in this House of Commons, and in fact and indeed casts an adverse reflection on every one of us.
I am convinced that certain political attitudes in this country have been systematically whittling away at the credibility of private enterprise. Our government is about to reverse that trend. We believe that our laws are the tools to cope with illegal conduct by any businesses or individuals who would take advantage. These laws should be enforced and respected. But we must dispense with the current notion that the government must have a window on industry in order to "keep them honest". We hear that term quite often from some of our friends in the House and outside it. This approach does not work. It destroys the respect which private businesses must hold toward the government which sets the rules. We in the government intend to give individual initiative and opportunity to flourish once again and to stimulate the enthusiasm of all our citizens to take a stake, to share in the risks of building a better Canada.
1 would like to deal with a few special topics, Mr. Speaker, but I would prefer to carry on at eight o'clock. So, may I call it six o'clock now?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to take the floor once again to continue my presentation in reply to the Speech from the Throne. As I was saying before six o'clock, we have a serious problem in the country, a problem relating to distrust which many Canadians feel toward their government, and which governments within the country feel toward one another. The problem of distrust seems to permeate all the actions of government, at least of the government in office until May 22 of this year.
Now I should like to discuss a number of specific situations starting with the one which has been thoroughly debated and on which we have been thoroughly battered by members of the opposition, and that is the question of Petro-Canada. I should like to put the following question to the House: do we feel the private sector oil companies of this country have shown cause to be distrusted?
I put a question to the president of Petro-Canada a few weeks ago, and 1 think the answer he gave was very important. I asked the president of Petro-Canada if, on the basis of having a window on the petroleum industry, he had any cause to distrust or to suspect the motives of any of the private sector oil companies in the country, and he said that he did not. Further he indicated that he had nothing but the highest regard for the senior executive administration of the private sector oil companies in the country. That is an important observation which must go on record.
Many members of the House feel some concern as to what Petro-Canada has learned as a result of this virtuous "window on industry" by which they propose to have advantage. I have strong reasons to suspect that if one were to ask the president of Petro-Canada what special information it has obtained as a consequence of having this window on industry, one would be severely disappointed in the information one would receive.
A colleague of mine asked the president of Petro-Canada what Petro-Canada feels it can do better than any private sector oil company in the country. As 1 recall it, the answer was that there was nothing Petro-Canada could do better, in the interests of this nation, than the private sector can do; that the only difference is that Petro-Canada might do it faster. Of course that refers to the ability to bring on offshore resources and petroleum reserves more quickly than the private sector. Then that becomes a matter of price because, if the price is right, the private sector will do it equally as fast. But if Petro-Canada has access to subsidized capital to pursue such exploration, of course it can do it more quickly.
Hon. members of the House should ask themselves if Petro-Canada is really profitable. Hon. members of the opposition have told us how profitable Petro-Canada is. But 1 have an article from a recent issue of The Globe and Mail which indicates that in 1978 Petro-Canada reported a profit of $13.7 million. The equity value of Petro-Canada is $3 billion, so this total profit represents less than .5 per cent return on investment. I think that is atrocious, and certainly no private sector corporation could exist in the country with that rate of return on investment.
October 16, 1979

Also I should like to ask another question in the House this evening. Who owns Petro-Canada? We have heard a lot of comment to the effect that Canadians own Petro-Canada. The government of this nation extended $800 million worth of equity capital to Petro-Canada which we financed by adding to our debt, and not one nickel of interest has been returned to the Crown in relation to the $800 million. In addition to that, Petro-Canada borrowed $1.5 billion in order to acquire the assets of Pacific Petroleums Co. Does the House realize where this equity came from? It was issued in the form of term preferred shares to the private banking system of the country. They went to the United States and elsewhere to borrow that money. If members of the House want to delude Canadians into believing that we own PetroCan, they are fooling the masses. Petro-Canada is owned by multinational interests who have loaned $1.5 billion to this country, and the shares are held in the names of the private chartered banks of Canada.
If one reads a financial statement of Petro-Canada, one will find that it has assets of $3 billion and liabilities of $849 million to the Crown of Canada. Where is the difference? The difference is in the form of term preferred shares issued to private sector banks in the country. They are the ones who have title to Petro-Canada.
I must ask members of the House what their wish is? Would they prefer that the private chartered banks own the shares and borrow the money internationally, or would they prefer that Canadians have an opportunity to own a piece of Petro-Canada? I recommend that the House consider the importance of giving individual Canadians the option to purchase shares, to own a portion of Petro-Canada, and to accept a portion of the risk.
Also 1 should like to ask one final question. Should the Government of Canada be engaged in those profitable sectors of our economy in order to pay for the costs of the high risk areas where indeed the government must play a role? The hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) and the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Trudeau) have suggested that we should use the profitable portions of Petro-Canada to finance its losses. I say, rubbish. That is not the role of the Government of Canada. If that was the case, we would want to own the multinational grocery merchandising firms in this country which enjoy a good rate of return on investment, and we would want to own, indeed, all the profitable ventures in this country. 1 submit that it is private individuals who should own a stake in Petro-Canada. It should be a Canadian-owned corporation, and the return on investment should go to those Canadians who choose to participate.
With that off my chest, Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments in the area of fisheries. I think that it is important that we re-establish trust, as I have indicated earlier in my representation, among the government, the bureaucracy, and the people affected by the decisions made by the bureaucracy. In the area of fisheries there has been a dismal record indeed, wherein decisions were taken within the bureaucracy
The Address-Mr. Siddon
with the consent of the minister, and after the fact those decisions were reported to the fishermen. That must change.
It is time that we instituted a policy of consultation. Since the appointment of the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), as Canada's Minister of Fisheries and Oceans a large number of initiatives have been taken to improve federal-provincial relations in the administration of our fisheries, and to improve relations with the canning industry, fishermen, and other fishing related industries. For example, the minister has recently met with the Atlantic fisheries council of provincial ministers and the Pacific fisheries council of provincial ministers. This is a first in many, many months, if not longer.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has announced that a major review of fisheries policy in Canada will be undertaken and presented to this House in the form of a white paper, with the participation of the provinces, fishermen, and the fishing industry. That is a first. The minister also indicated that the difficult questions of licensing and the recommendations of the Sinclair Report and Levelton Report will be subject for discussion and debate by the parliamentary Standing Committee on Fisheries and the Environment.
Such action is an expression of this government's willingness to involve all members of parliament in debate and discussions on issues of importance to that very important sector of our economy. The new Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has taken initiatives that were long overdue. I would submit that in many other areas of our government similar initiatives will be taken, and that we will be using all the resources of Parliament and inviting the input of all points of view in order to evolve policies in the interest of Canadians and in the interest of maximizing the return of those very abundant resources which we enjoy in the great country of Canada.
On the questions of energy policy there have been committees formed which have worked diligently through the summer, and a national energy policy should be forthcoming soon. That policy will deal with the short-term problems of security, of supply and incentives to conservation. In the mid-term a policy will be introduced which will find ways to ensure that the seven or eight oil sands plants and heavy oil installations are brought on stream by 1990 in order to make this country self-sufficient in energy. That policy will also address the question of long-term alternatives, not merely restricted to nuclear power, but including the consideration of a number of other very attractive alternatives.
We have reason for nothing but optimism relative to the future of our economy and opportunities for young Canadians. If we are to tap those opportunities we must make a special attack on the question of increased support for research and development in this country. It is long overdue that we stop all the platitudes and get down to finding a formula that will ensure, at least in the immediate future, that 1.5 per cent of our gross national product is re-invested in science and technology, and in the long run a level approaching 2.5 per cent. If it requires that we insist upon research and developmental technology content in foreign investment in Canada to the tune of 1.5 per cent, then we must insist upon it. And if we must

October 16, 1979
The Address-Mr. McCauley
insist that companies investing in Canada extend world product mandates for the products of our technology, then those are initiatives that we must take.
Finally, in relation to science and technology, I would suggest that the universities of this country are an important training ground. I spent ten years of my life in a university in Canada in a technological area, and I have been appalled and astounded by the pitiful lack of support by the former government for science and technology. It is high time that we had a policy recognizing that fact. For every oil sands plant to be brought on stream, we may require as many as 3,000 engineers and many other technical people. We must provide the training for those people and recognize that, if we do not accept that challenge now, we will be importing those technologies later.
Before 1 conclude, 1 would like to say that there has been a tremendous preoccupation in this country with programs of equalization DREE, U1C, welfare and all the other programs which have granted subsidies and special initiatives to various parts of this country. These programs have been overlapping and filled with redundancy. When we in this government introduce a program such as our scheme of mortgage credits, it is designed to benefit the people who have been footing the bill for all these other programs. It is high time that these people obtained a few concessions from this government.
In conclusion, what the Prime Minister was saying in this House was that we must restore mutual trust in one another, not only here in Parliament but in all the institutions of this nation and in the attitude of people toward this government. Trust is bred by a spirit of good will and a penchant for openness, tempered by a healthy respect for the other person's point of view. It is achieved by making a genuine effort to gather all the facts, not just some of the facts, by discussing our differences and arriving at an honest consensus.
I see that process as being a catalyst and also the consequence of initiatives set out in the throne speech. I hope to look back on the Thirty-first Parliament of Canada as a success story in re-establishing trust among Canadians.
